Italy had left the Axis and now sought its place in the peace. Kirk watched that bid from Rome. His report was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

An ambassador's report from a former enemy capital carried special weight. Italy's fate was on the conference's wider agenda. Readers get Rome's mood as the summit decided questions Italy could not vote on. The document shows a skilled envoy framing his host country's hopes for Washington's eyes.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d863:
Foreign secretaries at Potsdam received this report from the Economic Sub-Committee on July 20, 1945. The sub-committee had studied a United States memorandum on the economic principles for treating Germany in the first control period. It also weighed an annex on reparations. The report records both agreement and one sharp split.

The members agreed to urge adoption of the economic principles as drafted. They split on paying for German imports. British and American members wanted approved imports to rank as a first charge on German exports. Soviet members wanted reparation deliveries paid first instead. The report also notes disputes over Germany's 1937 borders and over which topics belonged to the sub-committee at all.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d963:
This undated paper, apparently a Soviet draft, restates the reparations bargain taking shape at Potsdam in late July 1945. Soviet claims would be met by removals from the Soviet zone. The USSR would settle Poland's claims from its own share. American, British, and other claims would be met from the western zones.

The USSR would also draw two shares from the west. Fifteen percent of usable surplus equipment, chiefly from metal, chemical, and machine plants, would be swapped for equal value in food, coal, and other goods. Ten percent more would pass free, as reparations. Removals must finish within two years, and the amount must be fixed within six months.
frus-1958-60v19-d63: China policy in the late 1950s runs through this FRUS memorandum from an assistant secretary. The State Department's China hands laid out their thinking. The document preserves that memo for historians. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
galileo-dialogo-bernegger-1663:
Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems appears here as Systema Cosmicum, in Matthias Bernegger's Latin translation, in the 1663 reprint. Galileo published the Dialogue in Italian in 1632. The book's defense of the Earth's motion led to his trial and condemnation in 1633.

Three speakers debate the Ptolemaic and Copernican systems over four days, with the Earth-centered view given the weaker voice. Bernegger's Latin carried the banned book to scholars across Europe who had no Italian. No public-domain English translation was located for this entry, so the text stands in Latin. The volume preserves the form in which learned Europe argued over the heavens.
gao-gaoreports-b-295463: MTB Group took its February 2005 loss to GAO, and the ruling issues the judgment. The firm's grievance went before the referee. Every protester gets judged on the merits alone. The merits decided it. The judgment was fair. The loss was reviewed.
gao-gaoreports-b-306663: Contractors collecting fees at agency conferences got a fiscal ruling in this January 2006 GAO call, which tests the practice. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the fee collection was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-400163: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Commonwealth Home Health Care, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-363: The FBI's enterprise architecture was underway in 2005, and GAO's report says the bureau was taking steps, though much remained. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the crime-fighting tech deserved a blueprint. The work had to be completed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-463: Census count corrections needed improving in 2005, and GAO's report says better efforts could produce more accurate data. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the headcount deserved accuracy. The efforts had to be improved. The headcount deserved accuracy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-563: School junk food was widely available in 2005, and GAO's report says competitive foods generated substantial revenues for schools. The findings do the math. The report warns that the students deserved healthier choices. The foods had to be understood. The students deserved healthier choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-663: Airport inspection staffing models needed improving in 2005, and GAO's report says the model for international passenger inspectors could be better. The findings demand the math. The report warns that the arriving travelers deserved smooth screening. The model had to be improved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-163: Run-down senior housing got a GAO look in 2006, and the report tours the troubled homes for the old and disabled. The findings show the decay. The report warns that the frail residents deserved decent roofs. The homes had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-263: National park air tours needed flexibility and enforcement in 2006, and GAO's report says both were required. The findings demand the balance. The report warns that the scenic skies needed fair rules. The enforcement had to be better. The scenic skies needed fair rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-363: The Senate restaurants' fund got audited for 2005 and 2004, and GAO's 2006 report delivers the financial opinion. The findings grade the books. The report shows even the Capitol's cafeterias got counted. The audit kept the books honest. The cafeterias' books were audited.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-63: Bowel disease care got a GAO check in 2006, and the report looks at what the health programs paid for in treatment and gear. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the suffering patients deserved fair care. The care had to be fair.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-963: The college antitrust exemption was not moving tuition in 2006, and GAO's report says schools' use of the exemption had not much affected affordability. The findings deflate the hopes. The report warns that the price-fixing pass was not the tuition villain. The exemption was not the answer.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-163: The Pacific compacts were straining in 2007, and GAO's report says Micronesia and the Marshall Islands faced sustainability and planning challenges. The findings map the troubles. The report warns that the island nations needed firmer footing. The friendship had to be funded wisely.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-463: Anesthesia pay had a two-tier problem in 2007 — GAO's report compares what Medicare and private plans paid for putting patients under. The findings expose the payment gap. The report quietly asks whether the public program's stinginess was squeezing the specialists it needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-563: Charity status was shielding tax cheats in 2007 — GAO's report finds thousands of tax-exempt groups owed nearly a billion in payroll and other taxes. The findings strip the halo off the scofflaws. The report asks why the tax collector went soft on the nonprofit set.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-763: Oil tanks above ground got an economic once-over in 2007 — GAO's report eyes the EPA's cost math for spill-prevention rules. The findings test whether the agency's numbers held water. Behind the spreadsheets sits the real question: who pays to keep the next spill from happening?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-863: Washington's wild lands were heating up in 2007 — GAO's report says federal land managers needed a real playbook for the changing climate. The findings press agencies to write the guidance before the fires, floods, and thaws wrote it for them. Public acres, the report argues, deserve a climate plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-163: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on audits of Public Companies: Continued Concentration in Audit Market for Large Public Companies Does Not Call for Immediate Action. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-263: The Government Accountability Office dug into department of Homeland Security: Better Planning and Assessment Needed to Improve Outcomes for Complex Service Acquisitions in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-463: The Government Accountability Office dug into financial Audit: Senate Restaurants Revolving Fund for Fiscal Years 2007 and 2006 in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-63: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report telling the State Department it needs transparent cost estimates to justify passport execution fees — the charges applicants pay when applying in person. GAO found the department's fee decisions lacked clear cost backing. The report argues that fees charged to millions of Americans should rest on documented numbers, not opaque calculations.
gerald-wales-historical-works-forester-1:
Gerald of Wales was a twelfth-century churchman who traveled Ireland and Wales and wrote about both with gusto. Thomas Forester translated his works for Bohn's series in 1863. This volume gathers the Topography of Ireland, the Conquest of Ireland, the Itinerary, and the Description of Wales.

Gerald reports strange beasts, wonders, and werewolves along with roads, rivers, and battles. He gossips, he moralizes, and he keeps a sharp eye on everything he passes. His Wales and Ireland are the wild Celtic fringe as a keen insider-outsider saw them. Few medieval travelers write with such life. Forester's one-volume gathering remains a handy door into Gerald's world.
greg-the-creed-of-christendom-its-founda: The Creed of Christendom, its foundations and superstructure, Greg's 1863 work. The doubter's creed. This book preserves that book. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
hawthorne-our-old-home-1863:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published Our Old Home in 1863, his English sketches from the Liverpool consulship. Hawthorne served as American consul at Liverpool from 1853 to 1857 under President Pierce, his friend. The book is the great American writer's reckoning with England, fond and sharp by turns here.

He sketches Liverpool docks, London streets, Oxford colleges, and the homes of poets he revered in England. English food, weather, and reserve get the same keen eye he gave Salem's Puritan past in fiction. A workhouse child who clung to him haunts the brightest of these travel pages with pathos. War at home made some passages sting English readers who expected pure praise from an American consul. The sketches show Hawthorne the observer, freed from romance plots, at his most humane.
home-incidents-in-my-life-1863:
Daniel Dunglas Home tells of his own marvels in Incidents in My Life, his book of 1863. Home was the most famed seer of his age. Lords and kings sat in his dark rooms. He was said to float out of a high pane and in at the next, while guests watched in awe and fear.

Home prints tales of cures, sounds, and forms in his calm, proud voice. He was ne'er caught in fraud, which set him past his peers. Fans and foes still row on what he did. His own book is the chief source.
howitt-history-supernatural-1863:
William Howitt swept all ages for marvels in The History of the Supernatural, his vast book of 1863. Howitt was a scribe of note who held the faith with zeal. Ghosts, dreams, witch hunts, seers, and saints fill two tomes. He draws from each land and age to show such things are no new craze, but a thread through all man's past.

His aim is plain: if all ages saw them, they must be true. Foes call the hoard a mix of gold and dross. Fans call it their vast store. It is the faith's own past of all pasts.
huxley-mans-place-in-nature-1863:
Thomas Henry Huxley, the biologist nicknamed 'Darwin's bulldog,' published Evidence as to Man's Place in Nature in 1863. It was the first book to apply Darwin's theory openly to human ancestry. Huxley wrote for readers ready to follow bones and brains wherever they led.

He compares the skeletons of men and apes bone by bone, and the brains organ by organ. The gap, he shows, is smaller between man and ape than between ape and lower monkeys. He also reviews the Neanderthal skull and the fossil finds of his day. The book made human evolution a public fight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mani-elijah-103:
Elijah Mani, a Turkish rabbi who ended his days at Hebron, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A native of Bagdad, he was esteemed there for his piety and his knowledge of the Cabala. About 1856 he went to Jerusalem. Two years later he settled in Hebron. He died there in the summer of 1899.

The article describes a rabbi who refused pay. When Rabbi Moses Pereire died, Mani succeeded him as rabbi of Hebron's Sephardim. For fourteen years he accepted no salary for the post. Poverty at last forced him to overcome his scruples. He stayed active in charity and communal affairs all the same. His simple, noble life won the respect of the whole ancient city. Muslims as well as Jews crowded his funeral. He is said to have written eleven works, and he refused to publish any of them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maskileison-nap:
Naphtali Maskileison, a Russian Hebrew author and book dealer, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 from Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman. Born at Radashkovichi, near Minsk, on February 20, 1829, he was taught Talmud by his father Abraham, the scholar of the previous generation. Poetry by Moses Luzzatto and Naphtali Wessely turned him toward modern Hebrew literature, which his Orthodox neighbors distrusted. He died at Minsk on November 19, 1897.

His first published work, a drama called "Esther," won praise from the poet Lebensohn, and his poems and essays appeared in Hebrew periodicals for forty years. His most valued labor was editorial: a corrected edition of Heilprin's chronicle "Seder ha-Dorot," whose tangled dates he put in order. The entry closes by calling him the best type of the Maskilim, the enlightenment's Hebrew men of letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendelson-morri:
Morritz Emanuilovich Mendelson, a Polish physiologist in Russia, is entered by Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Warsaw in 1855, he studied medicine at its university and took his Kharkov doctorate in 1884. For a decade after 1876 he trained in laboratories across Europe. At Berlin he worked under Dubois-Reymond; at Erlangen, under Rosenthal. At Paris he worked under Charcot at the Collège de France, serving for a time as assistant. From 1890 he was privat-docent in physiology at St. Petersburg.

The works the article lists, all in French, belong to the experimental physiology of muscle. They treat the lost time of muscles and the latent period of excitation, studied clinically. They treat the action of veratrine, and the excitability and mechanical work of muscle. They were published between 1879 and 1883 in the proceedings of the Collège de France and the Academy of Sciences.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-sara-baro:
Sara Meyer, later Baronin von Grotthusz, was a Berlin writer and salon hostess of the late eighteenth century, profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and S. J. Levinson. She wrote stories, plays, and essays on politics and morals in German and in French. Goethe, Lessing, and Schiller were among her friends and correspondents.

Most of those famous letters burned by accident; twenty-one from Goethe, written between 1797 and 1815, survived and were later published. The entry is frank about her faults, calling her light-minded, vain, and easily flattered. After her first marriage ended she was baptized and wed Baron von Grotthusz, dying at Oranienburg in 1828; her sister Mariane is sketched alongside her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minski-nikolai-:
Nikolai Minski, born Nikolai Wilenkin at Glubokoye in 1855, took his pen name from the town of his schooling, as Herman Rosenthal and N. Rashkovski write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At twelve he moved to Minsk and its classical gymnasium. His literary career opened in 1876 with Na Rodinye, a poem that at once attracted attention.

The poem, published in Vyestnik Yevropy — the journal that carried most of his verse — answered the sufferings of the Bulgarians in the Russo-Turkish war. Minski meanwhile read law at St. Petersburg, graduating in 1879. The entry places his formation in the progressive ferment of the era, which stirred his Jewish circle as much as Russian society at large.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montezinos-libr:
The Montezinos Library is the great private Judaica collection that became part of Amsterdam's Portuguese Rabbinical Seminary. Joseph Jacobs and I. George Dobsevage describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. D. R. Montezinos, the Amsterdam collector born in 1829, left it to the seminary in 1889. The seminary enlarged its building to receive it. It dedicated the library in April 1891.

The shelves hold twenty thousand volumes of Hebraica and Judaica. They include very early printed books and some seventy volumes of responsa. There are over a thousand pamphlets and about three hundred portraits of famous Jews. Some rare items in it appear in no bibliography. Montezinos had long taken charge of the seminary's library. Once his collection was merged into it, he supervised the arrangement of the whole.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-b-asher-1:
Moses ben Asher was a Masorite of Tiberias in the second half of the ninth century. Wilhelm Bacher wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He came from a line of Masorites reaching back to Asher the Elder, and he was the father of Aaron ben Asher. Scholars have debated whether the family were Karaites or followed rabbinic Judaism.

The entry comes down on the rabbinic side of that question. Its key evidence is a codex of the prophetical books completed by Moses at Tiberias in 895. The codex, kept in the Karaite synagogue at Cairo, carries Masoretic passages later ascribed to his son Aaron. Such short notices preserve the family history behind the Masoretic text of the Hebrew Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naboth-lit-frui:
Naboth was a Jezreelite whose vineyard stood beside King Ahab's palace at Jezreel. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn tell his story in the Jewish Encyclopedia, from First Kings. Ahab wanted the vineyard for a garden of herbs and offered a better one, or money. Naboth refused: it was the inheritance of his fathers.

Jezebel then forged the king's name in letters to the elders of Naboth's city. Two hired witnesses swore that Naboth had cursed God and the king, and he was stoned. His sons perished with him, and Ahab took the vineyard. The story stands in Scripture as the classic case of royal theft dressed up as law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-b-labi-b: Nathan b. Labi was a German writer on Jewish worship. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the start of the fourteenth century. His work, Sefer Mahkim, was also quoted as Sefer ha-Minhagim. The book was never published, yet later writers on worship used it often. Two copies of the manuscript survive, one in Vienna and one in Hamburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neufeld-daniel-:
Daniel Neufeld was a Polish writer for Jewish readers. Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Praszka in 1814. He died at Warsaw in 1874. His work centered first on Praszka and Chenstokhow.

In 1861 Neufeld settled in Warsaw to write. That year he published on Paris's Great Sanhedrin of 1806. He also launched Jutrzenka, a Polish weekly for Jews. It ran from July 1861 until 1863. He turned Genesis and Exodus into Polish, with commentary. He wrote on a Jewish consistory for Poland too. His Polish prayer book and Haggadah came in 1865. His daughter Bronislawa became a Polish writer herself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nomaus-of-gadar:
Œnomaus of Gadara was a pagan philosopher of Hadrian's age. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Ludwig Blau for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He belonged to the school of the younger Cynics. His book attacked the pagan oracles with force. Julian later blamed him for killing reverence for gods.

Grätz identified him with the Talmud's Abnimos ha-Gardi. His friendship with the tanna Meïr supports that view. Pagans once asked him how to get at the Jews. Visit their schools, he answered, and hear the children. While children chirp over the Doctrine, you cannot. Meïr condoled with him at his mother's death. Their riddling talks were prized as speeches of wisdom. His good conduct toward Jews, not his system, won rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oria-11763:
Oria is a city in the south of Italy. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It holds one of the oldest Jewish groups in Europe. A tale by Ahimaaz ben Paltiel sets his kin there. His forebear Amittai lived at Oria as early as 850.

Amittai's son Hananeel held a debate there in 880. His foe was the archbishop of Oria, a Christian chief. Jews at Oria read the Talmud and deep thought. They read Greek and Latin and the lore of drugs. Shabbethai Donnolo, a first Hebrew author, was born there. He was born at Oria in the year 913. In 925 Arab troops took the town by force. Ten scholars of the flock were slain in that attack.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palencia-hebrew:
Palencia is the chief town of its province in Spain. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It lies between Burgos and Valladolid, two old towns. A large, rich Jewish group settled there in early times. That group was there by the eleventh century.

The first ghetto was called Juderia Vieja, the Old Jewry. It lay by the church of San Julian, on the Carrion. So its Jews were called the Jews of San Julian. That ghetto soon grew too small for its folk in full. A new one, Juderia Nueva, rose by the great church. From 1185 the Jews stood under the bishop's guard. He took half of all the tax they paid each year. In 1291 their poll tax came to a great sum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pe-11963:
Pe is the seventeenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name seems to come from peh, the Hebrew word for mouth. The letter serves as a root, never as a prefix. It belongs with the labial letters.

Pe carries two sounds in Hebrew speech. With a dot inside it sounds like the English p. Without the dot it sounds like the English f. The letter also changes shape at a word's end. In the later counting system its value is eighty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesseles-joseph:
Joseph Pesseles was a leading Jew of Wilna in the 1700s. Herman Rosenthal and M. Garsson wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father was Rabbi Elias Pesseles of Wilna. The family backed the famed Gaon of Wilna for years.

Pesseles is known chiefly for one set of letters. In 1773 David Friedländer attacked Solomon Dubno in writing. Dubno had failed to oversee Mendelssohn's manuscripts as promised. Pesseles defended Dubno with warmth and calm. The letters show a rabbinic house open to new learning. That openness was rare in Russia then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinero-pinheiro:
Arthur Wing Pinero was an English playwright of Sephardic descent. Joseph Jacobs and Edgar Mels wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London on May 24, 1855. He first trained for the law in a solicitor's office.

The law bored Pinero, so he joined a theatre in 1874. Acting brought him little success under Irving. He turned to writing plays at speed instead. The Magistrate made his name for good. Sweet Lavender won hearts with its gentle pathos. Under Ibsen's strong spell he wrote The Second Mrs. Tanqueray.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pomis-de-12263:
De Pomis is the name of an old Italian Jewish family. Richard Gottheil, Ismar Elbogen, and Isaac Broydé wrote its history for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The family claimed descent from King David himself. A family tale says its first members came from Jerusalem to Rome. Titus is said to have brought four such families to Rome.

The family lived at Rome until about the year 1100. Its members then spread through Italy. Most settled at Spoleto in Umbria. There they stayed for more than four hundred years. In 1527 the army of Charles the Fifth sacked the region. The family fell into enemy hands and lost all it owned. David de Pomis told the family story in his own dictionary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-quirinius-p-sul:
Publius Sulpicius Quirinius was the Roman governor of Syria. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took that post in about the year 6. Great events and hard problems hang on his name. In that year Archelaus was banished from Judea. The land then passed to direct Roman rule.

Judea was joined to the province of Syria at that time. That link is why Augustus sent an ex-consul there. Quirinius was the man he chose for the post. Dio Cassius backs the date of the change, they note. The count of the people made in those years caused strife. The article works through the dates and the sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ranger-morris-1:
Morris Ranger was an English financier born in Hesse-Cassel about 1830. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He joined the Liverpool Exchange as a young man. He died at Liverpool in April 1887.

The article calls him once a huge cotton speculator. In one year his deals turned over nearly ten million pounds. He spent about a hundred thousand pounds a year on fees alone. Later his business failed. Ranger still took a leading part in Liverpool Jewish life. He gave freely and founded a university scholarship. The entry pairs great risk in trade with open handed giving.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reinach-12663:
Reinach is a German family that moved to France. Isidore Singer, Joseph Jacobs, and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The move came in the first half of the nineteenth century. The article profiles its most eminent members.

The sample opens with Jacques Reinach, a French financier. He held a stake in the second Panama Canal Company. In 1888 he helped win new concessions for it. In 1892 a newspaper accused him over publicity funds. Those funds were hinted to be bribes, the writers say. He was summoned but failed to appear. A warrant for his arrest followed. The next day he was found dead in bed. Suicide was suspected at the time. The entry then turns to Joseph Reinach.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rimmon-pomegran:
Rimmon is a name given to several places in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The word itself means pomegranate. The article sorts the places that share the name.

One Rimmon was a town of Zebulun on its northeast frontier. The Septuagint spells it more correctly as Rimonah, they say. It likely matches a Levite city given to Merari's sons. Its modern site may be Al-Rummanah near Nazareth. A second entry treats the rock Rimmon. Six hundred defeated Benjamites took refuge there after battle. A third is En-rimmon, a city of Judah. A fourth, Rimmon-parez, was a desert camp station. The entry keeps four same named places apart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-eduar:
Eduard Rosenthal was a German jurist born at Würzburg on September 6, 1853. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. He studied at Würzburg, Heidelberg, and Berlin, taking his law degree in 1878.

Rosenthal began teaching at Jena in 1880 as a privat-docent. By 1896 he was full professor of public law and German legal history. His books treat adultery under canon and German law in careful detail. Others cover town law, Bavarian courts, and railway freight rules across borders. He also wrote for a leading handbook of political science.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samegah-samigah:
Joseph ben Benjamin Samegah was a Turkish Talmudist and cabalist born at Salonica. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He died at Venice on June 6, 1629, as its rabbi and yeshibah head.

Before Venice, Samegah had headed the yeshibah at Padua in Italy. Hayyim Benveniste and Joseph Solomon Delmedigo ranked among his pupils there. His Mikra'e Kodesh, printed at Venice in 1586, treats all 613 commandments. One part covers love and fear of God, the other their hidden meanings. His Porat Yosef adds close novellae on Alfasi and the tosafot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-san-marino-1316:
Gotthard Deutsch and Amy A. Bernhardy wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on San Marino. The tiny republic in central Italy dates to the fourth century. Jews first appear in its records in the late fourteenth century. Statutes on debtors and moneylenders point to Jewish business there. In 1369 one Emanuele of Rimini lent money in San Marino.

The article follows the community through the republic's own archives. A Jewish banker, Musetto, supplied cash for princely visits in 1462. In the sixteenth century official documents grow numerous. A real community clearly existed by then. The government passed rules on Jewish trades again and again. Jews had to wear special badges and accept limits. Yet they also won official protection. In later centuries their numbers slowly shrank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schick-abraham-:
Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Abraham ben Aryeh Löb Schick. He was a Lithuanian Talmudist and author of the nineteenth century. Schick came from Slonim, in the government of Grodno. His special field was midrashic, or haggadic, literature. Nearly all of his books comment on such texts.

His Zera' Abraham, from 1833, comments on Midrash Mishle. His Me'ore ha-Esh, from 1834, edits the Tanna debe Eliyahu with notes and a long preface. His Maḥazeh ha-Shir, from 1840, comments on Canticles. His Eshed ha-Neḥalim, from 1843, comments on the Midrash Rabbot. His 'En Abraham, from 1848, treats Ibn Ḥabib's 'En Ya'aḳob. He also edited part of Jacob Dubno's Ohel Ya'aḳob in 1859. The entry maps a life spent opening old story texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sha-atnez-13463:
Sha'atnez is cloth made by mixing wool and linen in one fabric. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Mosaic law forbids wearing such a mix, in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. The Mishnah reads the word as a shorthand built from three Hebrew terms.

Those terms mean carded, woven, and twisted. The ban sits beside rules against mixing seeds or breeding unlike animals. Such mixing was seen as defying the order God set in nature. Maimonides linked the ban to avoiding heathen priestly dress. The entry shows how one clothing rule drew law, language study, and philosophy together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheol-13563:
Sheol is the Hebrew name for the place where the dead were believed to gather. Emil G. Hirsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the word. Its origin stays uncertain, the entry admits at once. Related words mean pit, destruction, and the deep abyss.

Jacob, grieving for Joseph, cried that he would go down to Sheol. Scripture places Sheol underneath the earth, very deep below. It lies at the farthest possible distance from heaven. The dead descend into it, and the revived rise from it. Hannah's song credits God with both movements. The entry gathers Bible verses to picture the shadowy underworld of ancient Israel, before later ideas of heaven and judgment took shape.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silva-antonio-j:
Antonio José da Silva was a Portuguese poet born in Rio de Janeiro in 1705. Isidore Singer and George Alexander Kohut wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied at Lisbon and Coimbra, taking his degree in 1726. That same year the Inquisition seized him at Lisbon.

He was charged with satirical poems and keeping Mosaic law. Torture left him unable to sign his own name. An auto da fé declared him penitent in 1726. He kept his old religion in secret afterward, though. Envious enemies accused him of relapsing into Judaism. In 1737 he and his wife were jailed again. Spies disguised as prisoners watched him in his cell. His wife died days before his own execution. He was burned at Lisbon's stake in 1739.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-isa:
Solomon ben Isaac of Orleans was a French tosafist of the twelfth century. Wilhelm Bacher and A Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the elder colleague of Joseph ben Isaac of Orleans. Together they signed responsa printed in Sefer ha-Yashar. Eliezer ben Joel ha-Levi quotes a joint responsum by both men.

Eliezer notes that he cannot tell if this Solomon is Rashi. That remark shows the two scholars were often confused. Solomon carried on a learned exchange with Rabbenu Tam. Tam addressed him by his full name or as Rabbi Solomon. The short entry preserves a case of two great names nearly merging.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spinning-13963:
Spinning and weaving are arts of extreme antiquity among all peoples. Emil G Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Egyptians were famed experts, making linen of silk-like softness. Mummy wrappings held threads of almost impossible fineness in count. One thread sixty miles long would weigh only one pound.

The raw materials were flax, sheep's wool, and goat hair. Camel hair was also used for tentings and mantles. Wool was washed hot, bleached, beaten, and carded by hand. All that work began as household labor for women. In later times wool carding became a distinct trade. The Mishnah says the wool carder was widely despised.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stork-karl-1406:
Karl Störk was an Austrian throat specialist born at Ofen in 1832. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on September 17 of that year. He studied at Prague and Vienna. He died at Vienna on September 13, 1899.

Störk earned his medical degree in 1858 at Vienna. That year he showed remedies could reach the larynx by laryngoscope. He invented several tools for treatment of the throat. He became a lecturer at Vienna in 1864. In 1891 he rose to professor and clinic chief. His books cover throat surgery and bronchial asthma. A later work treats diseases of nose, throat, and larynx. The entry marks a founder of modern laryngology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-synod-14163:
A synod is a council of rabbis and laymen that settles Jewish questions. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Such councils rule on doctrine, policy, and practice. Moses' elders form an early model for the body. The Great Assembly under Ezra offers another root.

One early synod under Hananiah fixed the Bible canon. It also compiled the official scroll of fast days. Medieval synods guarded Judaism and solved daily problems. Rabbi Tam led councils of hundreds at Troyes and Rheims. They ruled on civil cases under Jewish jurisdiction. One decree barred Jews from buying crucifixes for safety. Another softened the ban on polygamy for hardship cases. The entry traces self-government by council across centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theophany-14363:
A theophany is a visible showing of God to human beings. Kaufmann Kohler and M. Richtmann wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Strictly read, the Bible holds only four such scenes. A broader reading sorts them into three kinds. Some are told as history, some as prophetic vision, some as poetry.

The Sinai revelation anchors the historical kind. Thunder, lightning, fire, and trumpet blasts shook the mountain. From flame and cloud came the Ten Commandments. Deuteronomy retells the scene with care for God's lack of body. Deborah's song pictures the same God in storm. Habakkuk turns the coming of God into vivid verse. Isaiah and Ezekiel supply the vision kind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toulouse-hebr-1:
Toulouse, in southern France, had many Jews by the early eighth century. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. An old custom humiliated the community each Good Friday. Its most respected elder had his ears boxed at the cathedral. A plea to Charles the Bald in 850 failed to end it.

The custom ended only in the twelfth century. A yearly tax and wax payment replaced the blow. Thirteenth-century counts favored the Jews with land rights. Raymond VII let them sell and mortgage property freely in 1242. Philip the Fair later put Jewish cases before regular judges. Some Jews arrested in 1306 chose baptism over exile. Royal confiscations in the district reached huge sums.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ukba-mar-14563:
Mar Ukba was exilarch at Bagdad in the first half of the tenth century. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A revenue dispute set him against Gaon Kohen Zedek II. The calif Al-Muktadir deposed Ukba at his rival's urging. Ukba left Bagdad in 917.

In exile he won the calif's favor by poetry. He greeted the royal secretary daily with beautiful verses. The calif read them, summoned Ukba, and restored his office. Rivals soon deposed and banished him a second time. He fled to Kairwan in Africa, honored as royal seed. A throne-like seat was built for him in synagogue. He read third from the Torah scroll there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vellum-14663:
Vellum and parchment were the main writing skins of the ancient world. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Animal skins served as writing material across the East. Jews used them from Bible times onward. They grew highly skilled at preparing them.

The Talmud knew three kinds of skin material. Leather used the outside of the hide. Parchment used the inside. A third kind was scraped on both sides. Only skins of clean animals could serve for sacred books. Deer hide was the most common choice. Torah scrolls were usually written on full skins. The entry also notes Paul's mention of parchment books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-waldteufel-emil:
Emile Waldteufel was a French composer of dance music. He was born at Strasburg on December 9, 1837. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. His father, a working musician, taught him first. He finished his training at the Paris Conservatoire. Massenet was a fellow pupil and firm friend.

About 1860 poverty forced Waldteufel to leave his studies. He turned to waltzes, and one brought sudden fame. The Prince of Wales heard his waltz Manolo and praised it. English publishers then sought his work eagerly. In 1865 he became pianist to Empress Eugénie. He directed the court balls of Napoleon III. His waltzes ruled ballrooms across Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-werber-jacob-14:
Jacob Werber was an Austrian Hebraist and editor. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Brody on February 4, 1859. He died there on August 20, 1890. He was the son of Baruch Werber. At fifteen he already wrote fluent Hebrew.

In 1874 Jacob published a novelette of rare beauty. He wrote science pieces for Ha Maggid and Ha Zefirah. When his father died in 1876, he took over. He edited the family paper Ha Ibri until his death. Gravely ill in 1890, he wrote his own obituary. It appeared in the paper's last number. He died three days later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wittelshofer-le:
Leopold Wittelshofer (1818-1889) was an Austrian doctor who edited a top medical weekly. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Hungary, he took his medical degree at Vienna in 1841. He then practiced for ten years in Raab.

In 1851 he moved to Vienna for good. There he became editor of the Wiener Medizinische Wochenschrift. He wrote many essays for that paper over the years. He also wrote a book on the healing and aid sites of Vienna. That work came out in 1856. The entry is brief, but it marks his place in Austrian medical life. He linked hospital work with steady writing on care and health.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zangwill-louis-:
Louis Zangwill (born 1869) was an English novelist, the brother of Israel Zangwill. Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Bristol, he was schooled at the Jews' Free School. He taught at that school for a time as well.

He left that post with his brother in one act. The two set up a print shop as a firm then. In time he turned from print to tales of his own. He used the pen name Z. Z. on his books. His first book came out in the year 1895. Its Dutch scene and hue drew note from the press. Three more tales came in the next four years. They show a keen eye and a dry sort of wit. A late book treats its folk with a more warm heart. He ranks high as a chess man in his spare time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zin-15263:
Zin was a frontier post on the southern border of Judah, in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The books of Numbers and Joshua name Zin in their account of Judah's border. The line ran from the ascent of Akrabbim toward Kadesh-barnea.

The desert of Zin took its name from this place. Kadesh-barnea stood in that desert, and one verse calls the wilderness of Zin simply Kadesh. The entry weighs how nearby Paran fits the same reports. It places Zin just south of Judah, on high ground where the Azazime Bedouins then camped.
julius-caesar-pg2263: The Forum speeches duel in this edition: Brutus reasons, Antony weeps, and the mob turns. "Friends, Romans, countrymen" undoes the assassins' work. The tragedy of honorable men, and rhetoric's terrible power. Cassius's lean and hungry look has become proverbial.
kubark-interrogation-manual-1963:
The CIA taught its officers how to break a man's will to stay silent in a manual of 1963. KUBARK Counterintelligence Interrogation is that manual, long secret and now open to read. KUBARK was the agency's own code name for itself in its cables.

The book walks through the arrest, the cell, the threat, the pain, and the slow grind of question and reward. It sets out how to read a prisoner and how to time each kind of pressure. Later American interrogation doctrine grew from this text. Few Cold War papers show the spy craft of the age so plainly.
liber-monstrorum-haupt-1863:
The Liber monstrorum, the Book of Monsters, is an early medieval Latin work by an unknown author. Moriz Haupt's critical edition of 1863 supplies this text. In three books it lists monstrous peoples, beasts, and serpents, the marvels that early medieval readers placed at the edges of the world.

Some entries echo reports from Pliny and the Alexander tales. Others sound like garbled travelers' news given a Latin polish. The author now and then doubts his own reports, which makes the book feel honest. Haupt's edition fixed the text for modern study. It remains the Dark Ages' own field guide to the uncanny.
longfellow-wayside-inn-1863:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published Tales of a Wayside Inn in 1863, in the middle of the Civil War. He modeled the frame on Chaucer's Canterbury Tales: a company of friends at a real inn in Sudbury, Massachusetts, telling stories through the evenings. Longfellow knew the inn and its landlord well.

The landlord opens with Paul Revere's Ride, the midnight alarm of April 1775 that became the most recited poem in America. The other guests, a Sicilian, a Spanish Jew, a Norwegian musician, and more, answer with tales from their own traditions. Norse sagas, Italian novellas, and Jewish legends fill the three evenings. Longfellow's frame collection is his most genial book, a storyteller's gathering by the fire.
lyell-antiquity-of-man-1863:
Sir Charles Lyell, the great geologist of deep time, published The Geological Evidences of the Antiquity of Man in 1863. Lyell had long argued that Earth's rocks record vast ages. Now he turned that same slow clock on mankind itself.

He weighs flint tools found beside the bones of extinct beasts in caves and river gravels. Site by site, he builds the case that humans lived far earlier than the old chronology allowed. He also treats Darwin's theory and the ice ages. The book fixed human antiquity as a fact of science.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume four of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter twenty five. Canaples seeks to wed Mademoiselle de Vivonne, who has no fortune. The Cardinal de Coislin tells him he is too old to marry.

Her virtue draws a joke from the Cardinal that sets all laughing. The marriage, in the end, proves to bear no children. Then Saint-Simon tells of the Duc de Coislin and his extreme courtesy. Twice that courtesy puts his thumb out of joint in one tale. The guest locked the Duke in, and the Duke leapt from a window. Pride in manners becomes farce in Saint-Simon's dry telling.
memoirs-of-the-comtesse-du-barry-with-mi:
The Comtesse Du Barry's memoirs appear here in a second Gutenberg copy. The title promises minute details of her career as favorite of Louis XV. Baron Etienne Leon Lamothe-Langon stands as author on the title page.

An editor's note calls the work delightful and full of spice. It warns that the comtesse persona seldom tells the plain truth. Chapter one brings Lebel's letter and a second, fruitless visit. An invite to sup with the king changes her whole path at court. A supper, the first night, and the next day fill chapter two. Favor won fast must then be kept at a wary court.
nasa-tm-19720025000-cesium-diode-perform:
James F. Morris of the Lewis Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum in September 1972. His subject was cesium diodes, devices that turn heat straight into electric power. Morris gathered their test results from specialist conferences held between 1963 and 1971.

Rather than report one new test, the memorandum indexes and sums up many earlier papers. Lists name the materials used, the shapes built, and the working conditions tried. They also give outputs and working lifetimes for each design. A reader could find fast which diode setup fit a need. That made it a handy guide to early power work for space.
neckam-de-naturis-rerum-1863:
Alexander Neckam, an English schoolman of the twelfth century, wrote De naturis rerum, on the natures of things. Thomas Wright edited it for the Rolls Series in 1863. Neckam taught at Oxford, and his book gathers the natural knowledge of his age with a teacher's care.

Beasts, birds, winds, and waters pass under his review, each with tales and morals attached. He reports marvels beside plain facts, as his century expected. His sharp mind sorts what he can and repeats what he cannot test. The work shows medieval England learning about its own world. Wright's edition made this schoolman's survey a standard source for students of medieval science.
openalex-w1599703463:
S. Chatrchyan and the CMS Collaboration reported this measurement. It appeared in Physical Review C in January 2013. The team studied lead-lead collisions at the LHC. Charged particles do not fly out evenly in all directions. Their uneven pattern is called elliptic anisotropy here.

The team extracted the pattern with several cross-checking methods. They mapped it across momentum, angle, and collision types. Twelve classes of collision centrality were used in the study. Scaled results matched a shared pattern across systems, they found. That pattern held at varied energies and particle densities. The work supports a strongly flowing hot medium picture.
openalex-w205310263:
Marcela Tavares de Souza, Michelly Dias da Silva and Rachel de Carvalho explained the integrative review method. Their paper appeared in the journal Einstein in 2010. Health care needs practice based on solid evidence. The integrative review pulls many studies into one synthesis. It also shows how results apply in practice.

The authors present the method in six stages. First comes the guiding question. Then researchers search and sample the literature. Next they collect and judge the studies. Results are then discussed and presented. The paper draws on the authors' own review experience. It notes points that need care at each stage. The method helps nurses and clinicians use research well.
openalex-w2119130463:
Martha Anderson, William Kustas, John Norman and colleagues mapped daily water evaporation from land using satellites. Their paper appeared in Hydrology and Earth System Sciences in 2011. Evaporation data reveal drought onset and severity. Surface temperature from space shows soil moisture indirectly. Combining two satellite types can sharpen the maps.

Geostationary satellites watch the same area all day. Polar orbiters give finer spatial detail less often. The method fuses both data streams. It produces daily maps from field to continent scale. Farmers and water managers can use such maps. Drought monitors gain an early warning input. The approach was tested across varied landscapes.
openalex-w2139343763:
Laura Lamberti, Christa Fischer Walker, Adi Noiman, and colleagues published this review in BMC Public Health in 2011. They measured how breastfeeding protects babies and toddlers against diarrhea, a major killer of young children in poorer countries. Protection was compared across levels, from exclusive breastfeeding to none at all.

The team reviewed studies from 1980 to 2009 and pooled eighteen of them. Breastfeeding guarded against diarrhea illness, hospital stays, and deaths at every level studied. Exclusive breastfeeding protected young infants most strongly. Babies who were not breastfed faced many times the diarrhea death risk of exclusively breastfed babies. The findings back the World Health Organization call for exclusive breastfeeding for six months.
openalex-w2143305663:
J. Y. Liu, Yu-Jung Chuo, S. Shan, and colleagues published this study in Annales Geophysicae in 2004. They checked whether the ionosphere, the charged upper layer of the air, shows odd signals before large earthquakes. Their measure was total electron content, read continuously from ground receivers of the Global Positioning System.

The team set a rolling fifteen-day median as the normal reference for Taiwan. They then examined twenty earthquakes of magnitude six or more from 1999 to 2002. Odd signals appeared in the evening hours within five days before sixteen of the twenty quakes. That eighty percent rate suggests GPS electron data can register pre-earthquake ionosphere changes worth watching.
openalex-w2145474863:
V. Khachatryan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration published this study in the European Physical Journal C in 2014. They report the observation of the Higgs boson decaying into two photons. This rare decay gives a clean signal that lets physicists measure the Higgs mass with great precision.

The analysis used all CMS proton collision data from 2011 and 2012 at the Large Hadron Collider. A clear signal appeared near a mass of one hundred twenty-five billion electron volts. The measured mass came out just under that mark, with a small margin of error. The signal strength matched the standard model prediction within uncertainty. The team also tested spin models and split the signal by production route.
openalex-w2189079163:
Julian Homburger, Andrés Moreno-Estrada, Christopher Gignoux, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Genetics in 2015. They used genome-wide data to read the ancestry and population history of South America. The continent mixes Native American roots with later European and African arrivals, in patterns that differ sharply from country to country.

Samples came from over four hundred admixed people in Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Chile, and Argentina. Most European ancestry traced to the Iberian Peninsula, though many Argentines also traced roots to Italy. The Native American share formed a strong gradient tied to country and to the homelands of local indigenous peoples. Shared reference panels from four continents anchored the analysis.
openalex-w2269551063:
Henry Méndez, Georg Heimel, Stefanie Winkler, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2015. They challenge the standard story of molecular electrical doping in organic semiconductors. The usual view says a dopant molecule hands a whole charge to the host material, freeing a mobile charge carrier.

The authors show that a fundamentally different process can take over, depending on the host type. In small-molecule materials, dopant and host can lock together into charge-transfer crystallites, tiny ordered crystals with shared charge. These crystallites themselves act as the electrical dopants. The result matters for organic lights, solar cells, and transistors, where controlled doping makes devices work and design rules had assumed one mechanism only.
openalex-w2321443763:
Hazem Kalaji, Anjana Jajoo, Abdallah Oukarroum, and colleagues published this review in Acta Physiologiae Plantarum in 2016. They survey chlorophyll fluorescence as a way to watch plant health without harming the plant. Leaves re-emit a flicker of light during photosynthesis, and that signal betrays stress long before wilting shows.

Fluorescence readings report on photosystem II, the water-splitting engine of photosynthesis. They reveal the state of its reaction centers, light-harvesting antennae, and both electron entry and exit sides. The review gathers fast-fluorescence studies across drought, heat, salt, and other stresses. Portable meters now take the method outdoors. The authors see wide use ahead in crop breeding trials and field monitoring of stressed stands.
openalex-w2512047063:
Gabriella Morais Duarte Miranda, Antônio da Cruz Gouveia Mendes, and Ana Lúcia Andrade da Silva wrote this 2016 article on population aging in Brazil. It appeared in the Revista Brasileira de Geriatria e Gerontologia. The authors ask whether public policy is ready for a much older country. Their case study mixes national data systems with interviews from health and social policy actors.

In 2010 Brazil had thirty-nine older people for every hundred young people. By 2040 the estimate jumps to one hundred fifty-three per hundred. Interviewees said the country is not prepared, pointing to strains on pensions and health care. Older patients bring more disease, disability, and lasting effects, needing steady, team-based care. The authors urge the state to plan specific policies that protect quality of life in old age.
openalex-w2547739063:
Muhammad Awais Khan, Dorcus C. Gemenet, and Arthur Q. Villordon wrote this 2016 review in Frontiers in Plant Science. It surveys root system architecture in root and tuber crops such as cassava, potato, sweetpotato, and yam. Root shape decides how well a plant takes up water and nutrients and anchors itself. It also shapes how crops cope with drought and other stresses.

The authors note that root research on these crops lags far behind work on cereals. Most studies examine only the harvested storage root, not the whole root system. They describe how the root systems of the four major crops are built. Storage roots, they explain, grow from shoot-born roots rather than from a seedling root. Pulling this scattered knowledge together should help breeders shape roots that tolerate harsh growing conditions.
openalex-w2982538063:
Manuel Ramos-Casals, Pilar Brito-Zerón, Stefano Bombardieri, and colleagues issued these recommendations in Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases in 2019. They come from a task force of the European League Against Rheumatism, known as EULAR. The subject is Sjögren's syndrome, an autoimmune disease best known for dry eyes and dry mouth.

Treatment of this syndrome had barely changed in decades, with no target beyond easing symptoms. The task force set out to build the first EULAR guidance based on evidence and expert consensus. The recommendations cover both local treatments, such as drops and gels, and whole-body drug therapies. They give doctors a shared, current basis for choices that had long rested on habit and judgment alone.
openalex-w2984799663:
Karen de la Cruz-López, Leonardo Castro-Muñoz, Diego Reyes-Hernández, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Oncology. It examines lactate, a byproduct of sugar use, and its role in shaping the neighborhood around a tumor. That neighborhood, the tumor microenvironment, helps decide whether a cancer grows or stalls.

Tumor cells take in large amounts of glucose and release excess lactate even when oxygen is plentiful, a pattern first described by Otto Warburg in 1926. This metabolic shift is now counted among the hallmarks of cancer. Lactate does more than mark the shift: it regulates conditions around the tumor. The review covers that regulation and the treatment ideas that aim at lactate itself.
openalex-w3016898363:
M. Masiokas, A. Rabatel, A. Rivera, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Earth Science in 2020. It surveys the Andean cryosphere, the snow, ice, and frozen ground of South America's great mountain chain. Changes there can unleash hazards that threaten towns and works in the valleys below.

The authors describe current understanding of seasonal snow, glaciers, and mountain permafrost, with a focus on rock glaciers. They gather recent findings and set them against longer records to judge the direction of change. The picture matters far beyond high peaks, since Andean ice and snow feed rivers that millions depend on. The review closes by discussing open questions for the field.
openalex-w7204254663: Bleeding after childbirth kills mothers, and every minute of delay matters. This Spanish-language study tested whether putting the hemorrhage protocol on digital tools helped staff at a Sao Paulo public maternity ward follow it. Using a before-and-after design, the authors measured protocol adherence. A practical test of whether screens can save lives in the delivery room.
openalex-w7204994563: The teacher's job is being reinvented by technology, and this article studies what that means for the profession. Through qualitative literature research, the authors examine how social, cultural, and digital change is reshaping the teacher's role and identity, from knowledge-giver to mediator and guide. They focus on how teachers can build student autonomy in an education system in transition. Reflective and wide-ranging, it maps a profession in flux.
openalex-w7206168763: Alzheimer's disease begins damaging the brain years before memory fails, so early detection matters enormously. This literature review examines p-tau217, a protein fragment measurable in blood, as a potential early-warning marker for Alzheimer's. The authors summarize what research says about its accuracy and promise. If blood tests can flag the disease early, diagnosis gets cheaper and treatment can start sooner; that is the hope this paper evaluates.
openalex-w7214797263: Germs sense their world with special sensor proteins, and jamming them could stop infections. This paper mapped protein building blocks to design blockers for these germ sensors, starting from a natural mold compound. The team flagged strong leads. A drug-hunt study aimed at germs' sense organs.
plos-pbio-0020163:
Mazahir T. Hasan, Rainer W. Friedrich, Thomas Euler, and co-workers built a glowing sensor mouse in PLOS Biology in 2004. Their mice make fluorescent proteins that light up when calcium rises inside cells. Calcium spikes are a basic signal in nerve and muscle cells, so the glow reports cell activity.

A drug switch called TET control lets researchers turn the sensor on only when and where they want. That keeps the sensor from disturbing growth when it is not needed. With it, activity in living brain tissue can be watched under a microscope. The tool opened a path to watching whole circuits at work, a goal that later calcium imaging methods built on.
plos-pbio-0020363:
Bino John, Anton J. Enright, Alexei Aravin, and a large team predicted microRNA targets in humans in PLOS Biology in 2004. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that tune gene activity by binding to messenger RNAs. Each one may control hundreds of messages, but finding which ones was a fresh problem at the time.

The team wrote rules for spotting likely binding sites across human messages and tested them against known cases. Their target list gave the young field a map to work from. MicroRNAs are now known to shape development, immunity, and cancer. Early maps like this one set the terms for how targets are predicted and checked, and they remain a base that later methods refined.
plos-pone-0000063:
David G. Haskell, Jonathan P. Evans, and Neil W. Pelkey compared bird life across land uses in PLOS ONE in 2006. They surveyed birds in plantations, in forests, and in exurban areas, the low-density spread at a city's edge. Plantation land held far fewer bird kinds than the other two.

The authors call that bird life depauperate, thinned out. Forests held the richest mix, as expected, but exurban areas did better than plantations despite their houses and roads. The contrast warns that not all human land use is equal for wildlife. Tree plantations managed as single crops can be poorer habitat than lightly settled land. That ranking can guide land choices where birds are a concern.
plos-pone-0000163:
Frédéric Lemaire, Céline A. Mandon, Julien Reboud, and colleagues published this toxicology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It describes toxicity assays run in nanodrops, droplets so small that hundreds of tests fit in a tiny volume. The assays combine a living bioassay with morphometric endpoints, measurements of shape and form in the test organisms.

Small-scale tests use far less of a test chemical and far fewer animals. The authors show that nanodrop assays can still read out meaningful harm. The method points toward cheaper, higher-volume screening of chemicals and drugs, where testing capacity is often the bottleneck.
plos-pone-0000263:
Andreas Lamanda, Zeinab Cheaib, Melek Dilek Turgut, and colleagues published this biochemistry paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Proteins in saliva buffer acids, soaking up protons to protect teeth and the mouth. The authors study protein buffering in simple model systems and in whole human saliva, comparing the two.

Understanding saliva's buffering explains part of how the mouth resists acid attacks after eating. The authors measure how much of that protection comes from proteins rather than other components. The results have practical bearing on dental research and on designing artificial saliva for patients who make too little.
plos-pone-0000363:
Oren Kobiler, Assaf Rokney, and Amos B. Oppenheim wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study about lambda, a virus that infects bacteria. After entering a host cell, the virus faces a choice: multiply fast and burst the cell open, or stay quiet inside the host's DNA. Their work centers on one viral protein, CIII, that helps steer that choice.

CIII works by blocking a protease, an enzyme that cuts other proteins apart. By slowing that enzyme down, CIII helps tip the virus toward the quiet, dormant path. Working out how one small protein guides this switch helps explain how viruses balance attack and hiding, a basic question in virus biology.
plos-pone-0000463:
Gabriel del Rio and colleagues found a shared sequence pattern in a family of cell-death-related receptors, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dependence receptors are proteins that can trigger a cell to die when their partner molecule is absent. The team identified a novel motif, a recurring pattern of amino acids, in these receptors.

A shared motif is a clue to shared machinery: it marks the part of the receptor that likely does the common work. Motifs give biologists a handle for finding new family members in genome data and for guessing how the death signal is sent. Dependence receptors matter in development and in cancer, where their fail-safe killing can be lost.
plos-pone-0000563:
Eric Waltari and colleagues compared two ways of finding where species survived the ice ages, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Pleistocene refugia are the sheltered pockets where species waited out glacial cold. The team compared phylogeographic predictions, from DNA evidence, with ecological niche model predictions, from climate and habitat data, for locating those refugia.

Where the two methods agree, confidence is high; where they differ, each exposes the other's blind spots. Refugia matter now because they are often today's biodiversity hotspots and tomorrow's climate shelters. The study is a methods check with direct conservation use.
plos-pone-0000663:
Jack Merrin, Stanislas Leibler and John S. Chuang turned an inkjet printer into a tool for placing living bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many studies of interacting microbes need cells deposited in precisely defined patterns. Ordinary methods make that slow or costly. Their printer is piezoelectric, adapted from a design first built to print DNA microarrays.

The authors describe the device as inexpensive, and it can print patterns using multiple bacterial strains. Printing living cells like ink lets researchers set up microbial neighborhoods on purpose. Ecologists can then watch competition and cooperation unfold from known starting positions, a control that mixed cultures never offer.
plos-pone-0000763:
Michaela Frye, Amanda G. Fisher and Fiona M. Watt characterized skin stem cells by the chemical marks on their DNA packaging. Switching on the gene Myc pushes epidermal stem cells to leave their niche. They then turn into sebocytes and surface skin. The shift is tied to wide changes in gene transcription. Marks on histones, the packaging proteins, help set which genes can be read.

The team identified chromatin modifications characteristic of epidermal stem cells across the whole genome. Their title says these global marks define the stem cells, and that Myc-driven differentiation alters them. A signature of marks could let researchers recognize true stem cells without waiting for behavior.
plos-pone-0000863:
Murali Gururajan, Joshy Jacob and Bali Pulendran studied toll-like receptors in mouse B cells for PLOS ONE in 2007. Toll-like receptors are sensors that spot patterns found on germs and switch on the body's first line of defense. The team compared B cells from the spleen with B cells from mucosal tissue, the moist linings that meet the outside world.

For each cell group they asked which receptors are present and how strongly the cells respond when those receptors are triggered. The work maps immune sensing across two very different settings. It helps explain how B cells help start a broader immune response after they meet a threat.
plos-pone-0000963:
Ryan Nitta, Catherine Smith and Brian Kennedy tested how the retinoblastoma protein is broken down in cells missing certain lamins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lamins A and C are filaments that brace the cell nucleus. They are also needed to keep the retinoblastoma protein, a brake on cell growth, stable, though the route was unknown.

Two cancer linked proteins, gankyrin and MDM2, were natural suspects for the breakdown. The team report the loss runs through the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, but independently of both suspects. Ruling out the obvious routes is real progress. It tells the field where the true mechanism is not.
plos-pone-0001063:
Walter Weiss, Anita Kumar, George Jiang and colleagues tested a combined malaria vaccine in rhesus monkeys, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their earlier design used four antigens: DNA plasmids first, then a poxvirus boost. It protected a high percentage of monkeys against Plasmodium knowlesi malaria.

The vaccine covers several life stages of the parasite, including two blood stage antigens. This study asks how much protection depends on optimal DNA priming and on including those blood stage parts. Taking a working vaccine apart, piece by piece, shows which parts carry the protection. That knowledge is what lets a monkey success become a human candidate.
plos-pone-0001163:
Mucins are the main ingredients of mucus, and their genes contain long repetitive stretches that are hard to read. Yun Hee Jeong and colleagues examined one such gene, MUC2, in relation to stomach cancer, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The repetitive region, called a minisatellite, varies between people.

The authors report that rare versions of this repeat region influence susceptibility to gastric carcinoma. Mucin genes are well studied for how much protein they make, but their genomic variation is murkier because the repeats resist standard analysis. The study shows that even awkward repetitive DNA can carry disease risk.
plos-pone-0001263:
Keeping time, judging how long things last, depends on a network that includes the basal ganglia. Christian Beste and colleagues studied time processing in Huntington's disease, where the basal ganglia deteriorate, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Timing processes were already known to change in the disease.

This group-control study compared timing performance in Huntington's patients with healthy controls. Because the structures important for timing are also critical for the movement problems of Huntington's, the work links two features of one disease. Results like these can serve as sensitive measures of how the disease progresses.
plos-pone-0001363:
For HIV-positive mothers in low-resource settings, breastfeeding is often the only safe feeding option, yet it can transmit the virus. Louise Kuhn and colleagues followed mothers and infants in Zambia to study exclusive breastfeeding, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Clear data on the benefits of exclusive breastfeeding for HIV prevention were needed to encourage breastfeeding support programs.

The authors report high uptake of exclusive breastfeeding and reduced early post-natal HIV transmission where replacement feeding is unsafe. Mixed feeding had been thought riskier than exclusive breastfeeding; their data support promoting the exclusive pattern. The findings influenced infant feeding guidance for HIV-infected women.
plos-pone-0001463:
Zhiping Wang, Shicui Zhang, and Guangfeng Wang wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how fish eggs fend off germs. Fish that lay eggs in open water leave them amid dense microbes. How the young live through those attacks was not known. The team tested the fluid inside fresh zebrafish eggs.

They show the egg fluid can kill germs on its own. The killing comes from defense parts passed from the mother. That maternal guard covers the days before the young fish can make its own defense. The finding adds a neat chapter to how animals protect their young at the most frail stage.
plos-pone-0001563:
Alassane Dicko and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot for children in Mali. The shot blends proteins from two strains of the blood stage parasite. A past phase 1 trial in adults in Mali had cleared the way. This trial moved the shot into young children, the group at most risk.

The team checked safety and immune replies in the children step by step. A shot that is safe in adults can act unlike in young children. Child data are thus the true gate for a malaria vaccine. This trial is a key rung on that climb.
plos-pone-0001663:
P. K. Vinod, Neelanjan Sengupta, P. J. Bhat, and their co-authors mapped how three signaling pathways jointly control a yeast gene in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, adapts to its surroundings to survive. When nitrogen runs low, it grows in chains of stretched cells called pseudohyphae, which help it forage. The switch is driven by a gene named FLO11.

The study integrates the cAMP-PKA, MAPK, and TOR pathways, three major signal routes that sense food and stress. The full text gives the model, the gene activity data, and how each pathway's push on FLO11 adds up. Yeast is a stand-in for cells in general, so rules found here guide work on how cells combine signals to make one decision.
plos-pone-0001763:
Heather Sadlish, Heike Rampelt, James Shorter, and their co-authors studied helper proteins that manage yeast prions in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Prions are proteins that fold into self-copying shapes. In yeast they create heritable traits. The cytosolic chaperone network, the cell's protein-folding crew, is closely tied to prion emergence and maintenance. The Hsp110 chaperone Sse1 exchanges nucleotides for Hsp70 chaperones.

The team reports that Hsp110 chaperones regulate prion formation and propagation through two discrete activities. The full text gives the yeast experiments and the activity separation. Yeast prions are a safe stand-in for the protein clumping behind human diseases like Alzheimer's, so their control crew is studied worldwide.
plos-pone-0001863:
Uri Yerushalmi and Mina Teicher used computer simulations of evolution to study timing in neural processing in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Recent studies suggested some neural mechanisms rest on the fine timing structure of spiking activity, the exact timing of nerve spikes. Less effort had gone into how such mechanisms evolve: could they arise, and must they?

Running such simulations, the authors argue temporal elements in neural processing are inevitable: selection produces them without being asked. The full text gives the simulation setup and the evolved networks. If timing codes arise inevitably, then brain labs should expect them in all brains, not as rare inventions of certain brains.
plos-pone-0001963:
Akira Kinjo and Haruki Nakamura analyzed what makes a protein family's signature, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Labs spot distant kinship between proteins by comparing them to a position-specific scoring matrix, a table that scores each spot in a sequence. Those tables seem to hold the essence of a family, but what that essence is made of was unclear.

The pair applied singular value analysis, a math tool that splits a table into ranked parts, to many such matrices. Their aim was to see which parts carry the family stamp. Knowing the anatomy of a signature can make homology searches sharper and faster.
plos-pone-0002063:
Isabelle Lombaert and co-authors rescued spit glands with stem cells after radiation, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Head and neck cancer is the fifth most common cancer, and survival is fairly high. Yet radiation often wrecks the salivary glands, leaving patients with dry mouths and a much poorer quality of life.

The team transplanted stem cells into irradiated glands in their model. As the title states, the transplant rescued gland function after the damage. A working rescue in animals is a first step toward giving cancer survivors back a basic comfort that radiation takes away.
plos-pone-0002163:
Crystal Jaing, Shea Gardner, Kevin McLoughlin, and co-authors built a gene chip for spotting the weapons of harmful bacteria, described in PLOS ONE in 2008. Known and unknown germs pose a steady threat to public health, and fast tools to detect and describe them are badly needed. Existing tests cannot cover the full range of what makes a microbe dangerous.

The team's functional gene array carries probes for bacterial virulence elements, the genes that let bacteria cause disease. A single test can scan a sample for many such genes at once. Tools like this help health teams name a threat early, before an outbreak grows legs.
plos-pone-0002263:
Farrel Buchinsky, Joseph Donfack, Craig Derkay, and co-authors studied children and adults with a rare airway disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis grows wart-like tumors in the airway, causing hoarseness and trouble breathing. It is caused by human papillomavirus types 6 or 11, and its course varies hugely, with patients needing repeated surgeries to keep the airway open.

The team compared cases by HPV type and by age at diagnosis. They report that the child's age, more than the virus type, tracks with how the disease behaves. That ordering helps doctors counsel families on what course to expect.
plos-pone-0002363:
Ted Cohen, Caroline Colijn, and Bryson Finklea asked whether surveys understate the burden of drug-resistant tuberculosis, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. TB strains resistant to many first- and second-line antibiotics challenge a global strategy built on standard drug regimens. Highly resistant strains had already been blamed in outbreaks. Survey-based estimates guide the money and drugs sent to fight them.

The team used a simulation study to test how those estimates are built. Their modeling suggests survey methods can miss part of the true burden, for instance where resistant cases die or are treated outside the system. Getting the count right decides whether control programs are sized for the epidemic they actually face.
plos-pone-0002463:
Stjernman joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Martin Stjernman, Lars Råberg, Jan-Åke Nilsson, among others. Its subject is maximum Host Survival at Intermediate Parasite Infection Intensities. Although parasitism has been acknowledged as an important selective force in the evolution of host life histories.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002563:
Corcoran led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Kelly E. Corcoran, Katarzyna A. Trzaska, Helen Fernandes, among others. Its subject is mesenchymal Stem Cells in Early Entry of Breast Cancer into Bone Marrow.

BCCs can achieve quiescence, without interfering with hematopoiesis. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002663:
A 2008 study by Rafael Sanjuán and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up a network model for the correlation between epistasis and genomic complexity. Authorship is credited in the record to Rafael Sanjuán and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The study of genetic interactions (epistasis) is central to the understanding of genome organization and evolution. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002763:
