Lee Alan Dugatkin and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on cheating on the edge. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Lee Alan Dugatkin, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. We present the results of an individual agent-based model of antibiotic resistance in bacteria. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002863:
Bilada Bilican and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was induction of olig2 + precursors by FGF involves BMP signalling blockade at the smad level. The catalog record names Bilada Bilican first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. During normal development oligodendrocyte precursors (OPCs) are generated in the ventral spinal cord in response to Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signalling. It goes on to note a further point. There is also a second, late wave of oligodendrogenesis in the dorsal spinal cord independent of Shh activity. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002963:
Christopher Love, Shuguang Zhang and Andreas Mershin chased the source of a steady voltage in a potted fig tree in 2008. It has long been known that many plants hold an electrical potential between their xylem, the water-carrying tissue, and the soil. What creates that voltage stayed controversial for years.

After ruling out stray capacitive and inductive effects from the setup, the team probed the sustained difference in a Ficus benjamina tree. Published in PLOS ONE, the quirky study treats a textbook curiosity with care. Its results bear on claims that trees might serve as living power sources.
plos-pone-0003063:
Amit Bharadwaj, Sadhu Leelavathi, Sudeshna Mazumdar-Leighton and co-authors studied a heat- and alkali-tough enzyme in 2008. Understanding protein stability under several extreme conditions at once remains a major challenge. The xylanase from Bacillus sp. NG-27, called BSX, works best at high temperature and alkaline pH and resists denaturants.

A partly exposed valine at the protein's start plays a critical role in stabilizing it, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, one residue with an outsized effect is a neat lesson for enzyme engineering, where industrial users prize exactly this toughness. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003163:
Alma Fulurija, Thomas A. Lutz, Katja Sladko and colleagues test vaccination against the hormone GIP as an obesity treatment in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The World Health Organization counted more than one billion people worldwide as overweight and at risk of chronic illness, including heart disease, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and stroke. Current therapies showed limited efficacy and often had unpleasant side effects.

The authors explore blocking GIP by vaccination as a fresh route to weight control. Readers get a bold idea tested at an early stage. Even readers who doubt the approach will find the reasoning useful for judging obesity research claims.
plos-pone-0003263:
Lauren McDaniel, Mya Breitbart, Jennifer Mobberley and colleagues sequence viruses from Tampa Bay in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Phage integrase genes often play a role in establishing lysogeny in temperate phage, by catalyzing integration of the phage into one of the host's replicons. To investigate temperate phage gene expression, an induced viral metagenome from Tampa Bay was sequenced by 454 methods.

Readers get a metagenomic analysis of lysogeny, the state where a virus hides in its host, and implications for prophage gene expression. Coastal virus communities affect marine bacteria and carbon flow, so their hidden state matters to ocean ecology.
plos-pone-0003363:
Søren Søgaard Lund, Lise Tarnow, Anne Sofie Astrup and colleagues trial metformin in type 1 diabetes in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Despite intensive insulin treatment, many patients with type 1 diabetes have longstanding inadequate glycaemic control. Metformin is an oral hypoglycaemic agent that improves insulin action in patients with type 2 diabetes. The team investigated effect of a one-year treatment in type 1 patients.

Their randomized study tests adjunct metformin treatment in patients with persistent inadequate control. Readers get trial evidence on borrowing a type 2 drug for type 1 care. Even a modest insulin-sparing effect matters over a lifetime of injections.
plos-pone-0003463:
Heekyung Chung and co-authors measured mutation rates in repair-defective cells in this 2008 study. Some cells cannot fix mismatched DNA letters properly. In such cells, repeated short DNA stretches in genes mutate often. Two tumor suppressor genes, TGFBR2 and ACVR2, carry such fragile stretches.

Breaks in those genes cut off signals that restrain colon tumors. The team clocked how fast the coding repeats in each gene mutate. Direct rates help explain how colon cancers form in these patients. The numbers sharpen models of microsatellite-unstable cancer growth. Colon tumors with broken repair are a large and well studied cancer group.
plos-pone-0003563:
Xiao-Ning Zhang and co-authors studied early blue light responses in a plant in this 2008 paper. Cryptochromes are blue light sensors found across many life forms. They steer development and help set daily clocks. In Arabidopsis, cryptochrome 1 drives an early response to blue light.

A protein named HFR1 proved crucial for that first response. It helps regulate the whole set of genes reacting to the light. Without it, the early transcriptome response falters. The finding maps a relay between light sensing and gene control. Light is the main timing cue for plant growth in fields and forests.
plos-pone-0003663:
Rivka Inzelberg, Edna Schechtman, and Shraga Hocherman published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Visuo-motor coordination means turning what the eyes see into planned, guided movement. That chain needs thinking skills and motor skills, both of which Parkinson's disease impairs.

The team measured these coordination deficits in patients and set them beside their motor impairments. The results show where the chain between seeing and doing breaks in this disease. Such detail can guide therapy and tests that track how the illness advances beyond tremor and stiffness alone. Tests like these can also help track change over time.
plos-pone-0003763:
Kristoffer S. Larsen, Jing Xu, Silvia Cermelli, and colleagues published this cell transport study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cells move their inner cargo along microtubule tracks using motor proteins such as dynein. How that motor's activity is regulated was not well understood. The protein BicaudalD helps dynein do its job.

The team studied BicaudalD during the transport of lipid droplets, the cell's fat stores. They found it actively regulates the motor's activity rather than just linking cargo to track. The work shows how cells steer fat cargo with precision inside the cell.
plos-pone-0003863:
Rui Wang-Sattler, Yao Yu, Kirstin Mittelstrass, and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Smoking exposes the body to nicotine and causes a multitude of metabolic changes that are poorly understood. The KORA study is a large health cohort in the Augsburg region of Germany.

The team quantified 198 metabolites in 283 serum samples from the cohort. Comparing smokers and non-smokers revealed distinct variations tied to nicotine consumption. These first results show how deeply tobacco use marks the chemistry of human blood. Such profiles could one day flag harm from smoke sooner.
plos-pone-0003963:
Wenyan Zhang, Gongying Chen, Anna Maria Niewiadomska, and co-authors studied how HIV disarms cell defenses in 2008. Human APOBEC3 proteins can block many retroviruses, including HIV-1. To spread, HIV must suppress several of these defender proteins. Its Vif protein carries out that suppression.

Their PLOS ONE article maps which parts of Vif and APOBEC3 must meet. Distinct contact points are needed against different defender proteins. That detail shows how one viral protein handles a whole family of foes. Blocking those contacts could let natural defenses stop HIV again. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004063:
Akira Mamiya, Jennifer Beshel, Chunsu Xu, and co-authors recorded airflow sensing in fly brains in 2008. The mushroom body is a higher center in the Drosophila brain. It is best known for handling smell information. How its neurons respond to non-smell senses was not known.

Their PLOS ONE article characterizes mushroom body responses to airflow. Airflow is a key cue for a flying insect's orientation. Responses there suggest the center merges several senses, not smell alone. That merging may help flies link wind with odor plumes. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004163:
Jessica Stolze-Rybczynski and colleagues published this fungal study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most of the 30,000 known species in the group Basidiomycota shoot off their spores with a fluid droplet. The droplet, called Buller's drop, races across the spore surface and powers the launch. In yeasts, rusts, and smuts of the same group, spores are instead discharged straight into the air.

The team compared these discharge mechanisms and how they were adapted across the group. Tracing the changes shows how a single spore-launching trick was reshaped for different lifestyles. The study adds a mechanical chapter to the evolution of fungi.
plos-pone-0004263:
Hans Gross and colleagues published this bee cognition study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Numerical abilities have been studied in many vertebrates, but convincing accounts of number sense in invertebrates are few. Honeybees, with their many impressive cognitive feats, are prime candidates for such a test.

The team tested whether bees can generalise a visual task by number, applying a learned count to new images. Their study asks whether a bee's brain tracks how many items it sees, not just what they look like. A positive answer would show that number sense does not require a big brain.
plos-pone-0004363:
Pawan Gupta and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. TR2 is an orphan nuclear receptor expressed specifically in early embryos. It is a transcription factor that controls key stem cell genes, including Oct4, a master stem cell gene. TR2 can act as both activator and repressor in gene control.

The team describe HDAC3 as a molecular chaperone that shuttles phosphorylated TR2 to PML bodies, storage sites in the nucleus. They call this a novel, deacetylase activity-independent function of HDAC3, which usually edits gene activity chemically. A familiar enzyme moonlighting as an escort changes how TR2's targets get controlled.
plos-pone-0004463:
Two sulfur-bearing spots on a virus shell protein are vital for infection, show Samuel Campos and Michelle Ozbun in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is L2, a minor part of the shell of human papillomavirus type 16, a virus that can cause cancer. L2 does a job that is essential for infection, but that job was not well understood.

The two spots are cysteine residues, building blocks that can link to each other. The team showed they form a bond inside the L2 molecule, and that breaking them cripples the virus in human skin cells. A known target for antibodies sits near the same region. Together, the details sketch how L2 helps the virus enter cells, and where vaccines or drugs might block it.
plos-pone-0004563:
Melanoma cells answer a gene-awakening drug in varied ways that may predict who benefits, report Ruth Halaban, Michael Krauthammer, Mattia Pelizzola, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug is decitabine. It reactivates genes silenced by DNA methylation, a chemical mark that can shut genes off in cancer.

Decitabine helps some cancer patients but not others, especially those with solid tumors. The team carried out an integrative analysis of how melanoma cells respond at the epigenetic level, the level of marks rather than the DNA code itself. Patterns in that response carry clinical implications: they may separate likely responders from patients who would only suffer side effects. Such sorting is the heart of personalized cancer care.
plos-pone-0004663:
A growth factor shields salivary glands from radiation damage, show Kirsten Limesand, Sherif Said, and Steven Anderson in PLOS ONE in 2009. Radiation is a primary or secondary treatment for head and neck cancer. A common side effect of irradiation to the head and neck is xerostomia, severe dry mouth, caused by salivary gland dysfunction. Tens of thousands of new cases result from radiation treatment each year.

The factor is IGF-1, insulin-like growth factor 1. The team reports that it suppresses radiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction in their experiments. Preserving saliva is not a small comfort: it protects teeth, speech, taste, and eating. A protectant that can be given around radiation sessions would improve life for many cancer survivors.
plos-pone-0004763:
Caterina Longo and colleagues built core shell gel particles that catch and keep fragile blood markers, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Blood holds a rich set of early disease markers waiting to be found. Three hurdles block that search, the authors note, starting with the tiny amounts of most markers in blood.

Large common proteins swamp the signal, and markers break down fast after drawing. The new particles harvest rare markers, concentrate them, and protect them from decay. Better capture could make early disease tests far more sensitive. It may open marker hunts that now fail. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail.
plos-pone-0004863:
Hans Herfarth and colleagues studied frequency and nature of incidental extra enteric lesions on MR enterography in bowel disease, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The aim was to determine occurrence of extra enteric findings in a large cohort undergoing magnetic resonance enterography and classify clinical significance. The team retrospectively analyzed over a thousand examinations in about a thousand patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

Incidental findings are common and mostly benign. Some require urgent follow up care. Radiologists need clear reporting pathways. Patients benefit when scans check beyond the bowel. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004963:
For sperm to fertilize an egg, it must fire its acrosome. The acrosome is a cap of enzymes that helps sperm penetrate the egg's coat. Luis Federico Bátiz and colleagues studied a mouse defect in this step. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The mice carry the hyh mutation. It changes one building block in the protein alpha-SNAP.

Sperm from these mice have a defect in the acrosome reaction. The study traces that failure to the single mutation. A tiny genetic typo breaks the final step of fertilization. The work shows how sensitive the sperm's firing machinery is. It also gives researchers a precise model of one cause of male infertility.
plos-pone-0005063:
Gut germs influence diabetes risk in animal models. The mechanism behind that influence was murky. Paul Bollyky and colleagues named a relay in PLOS ONE in 2009. The relay is Myd88, an adaptor in the toll-like receptor pathway. That pathway senses microbes. The team tested Myd88's role in pancreatic beta cells.

Myd88 contributes to beta-cell homeostasis after injury. Without it, the insulin-making cells recover poorly. The finding ties gut microbes to the pancreas through an immune relay. It also reframes beta-cell health as partly an immune story. Diabetes research often treats these cells in isolation. This work shows their microbial environment matters. The relay could become a treatment target.
plos-pone-0005163:
Stare at a moving pattern and a still dot can vanish. The illusion is called motion-induced blindness. Po-Jang Hsieh and Peter Tse tracked the eyes during it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They measured microsaccades, tiny involuntary eye movements. They also measured eyeblink rates. Volunteers reported when the dot was visible or gone.

Microsaccade rate varied with subjective visibility. The eyes move differently when the dot is seen versus unseen. This was the first psychophysical data on the link. The eyes betray the mind's seeing. Such links help scientists study visual awareness itself. Awareness is hard to measure directly. Eye behavior offers an objective window into it.
plos-pone-0005263:
In Crohn's disease, the gut is inflamed, and certain chemokines, signals that call in immune cells, run high. One of them, CXCL10, tracks with disease activity. Grip and Janciauskiene tested in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether a statin drug could lower it.

Statins are cholesterol drugs that also calm chemokine production in heart patients. Patients with Crohn's disease who took atorvastatin showed reduced plasma levels of CXCL10, as the title states. The result hints that a familiar heart drug might also help soothe gut inflammation. A cheap pill used for years in heart care would be easy to test in gut clinics, since its side effects and safe dose are already well known.
plos-pone-0005363:
When E. coli DNA is damaged, the bacterium sounds an alarm called the SOS response. Two genes, recA and lexA, regulate each other in a feedback loop at its heart. Shimoni and colleagues analyzed the randomness of that circuit in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Gene circuits do not run like clockwork; molecule counts are small and noisy. A stochastic analysis treats that noise directly instead of averaging it away. The results show how a bacterium can mount a reliable alarm from unreliable parts, a core lesson in systems biology. Noise is not a flaw in the cell's alarm. it may let a few cells act fast while the rest wait, a spread of bets that helps a whole colony live through a hard hit.
plos-pone-0005463:
Konstantin Kadzhaev and colleagues hunted genes that make a germ dangerous, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Francisella tularensis is a germ that can cause severe and sometimes fatal illness in people. Its most harmful strains belong to one branch of the species.

Using mice infected through the skin, the team tested which germ genes are needed to cause disease. Each gene that proved vital is a clue to how the germ attacks the body. Such clues can guide the search for drugs or vaccines against a germ that is also feared as a possible weapon.
plos-pone-0005563:
Wenrui Duan and co-authors studied a mutant cancer gene in transgenic mice for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Changes in the gene p53 are among the most common faults in human lung cancer. One hotspot for those changes sits in the part of the protein that grips DNA.

The team built mice carrying that mutant gene in their lungs. They watched how lung tumours arose across the animals' lives and how the pattern changed with age. The model helps show how one famous gene fault drives lung cancer over time. Age shifts in tumour patterns matter because lung cancer is mainly a disease of older people.
plos-pone-0005663:
Moritz Wildgruber and co-authors used magnetic nano-sensors to track immune cells in artery disease in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Monocytes are blood cells that enter tissues and become defenders or healers. In people they come in at least two groups whose shares shift with heart disease, sepsis, and viral infection.

The sensors let the team profile those groups over the course of atherosclerosis in animals. Watching the groups rise and fall could one day guide treatment of artery disease. The method also promises faster blood tests from tiny samples. Heart artery disease remains a top killer, and blood cell groups that track it could guide care earlier.
plos-pone-0005763:
Abhay Sharma and Priyanka Singh tested a bold claim in fruit flies in 2009: that a father's gained traits can pass to offspring through sperm. Most known cases of such inherited effects involve exposures before birth or during sperm formation. Adult experience reshaping the germline was less established.

Using a Drosophila model, the team looked for gene-activity patterns from the father's brain turning up in the next generation via sperm. Any solid case would stretch the rules of inheritance. Their systems approach lays out the evidence and its limits, a useful base for a debated topic.
plos-pone-0005863:
Alexander Wittenberg and co-authors showed in 2009 that sex reshuffles the genome of a wheat pathogen to an extraordinary degree. Mycosphaerella graminicola is a haploid fungus that briefly turns diploid to produce spores. In that brief phase, matching chromosomes can swap parts.

Some chromosomes proved surprisingly dispensable or unstable through meiosis. That plasticity helps the fungus adapt fast to resistant wheat varieties and fungicides. It is bad news for breeders, but knowing the mechanism guides more durable resistance strategies. The paper is a striking case of genome flexibility in a plant enemy.
plos-pone-0005963:
Turning down one cell signal can stretch life in yeast, and perhaps in mammals too. Linda Enns, John Morton, Piper Treuting and colleagues tested that hope in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper disrupts protein kinase A, a signal enzyme, by removing one of its control parts, a change known to leave mice lean and sensitive to insulin.

The title gives the verdict: the mice aged in a healthier way. Healthy aging, as opposed to mere long life, is the prize most aging research now seeks. The work ties a single signal pathway to that prize in a mammal, and it gives drug and diet studies a target that has already passed a real test in mice.
plos-pone-0006063:
You cannot study appetite if you cannot measure a meal. Richard Wong, Matthew Piper, Bregje Wertheim and colleagues solved that basic problem for the fruit fly in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents a reliable way to measure how much food Drosophila eats while left alone, in steady conditions, in normal culture.

Earlier measures were unreliable or disturbed the flies they watched. A sound intake measure serves studies of behavior, nutrition and drug dosing, all of which lean on knowing the dose a fly truly ate. The method is a modest tool on its face, and a foundation for a large share of fly research.
plos-pone-0006163:
Prolactin was thought to be a mammal hormone until fish told a longer story. Xigui Huang, Michelle Hui, Yun Liu and colleagues discovered a novel prolactin in non-mammalian vertebrates in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper places the find in the hormone family that includes growth hormone and somatolactin, kin proteins with similar gene structure, and traces its role in the fish retina.

The new hormone takes part in teleost retina development, the title reports. A hormone family that predates mammals changes how its whole evolution is told. The fish eye also gains a growth signal to study, in an organ where prolactin's presence was itself a surprise.
plos-pone-0006263:
A harmless bacterium used in some immune therapies needed its identity settled. Vikram Saini and colleagues studied Mycobacterium indicus pranii in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their polyphasic taxonomic analysis combined many kinds of evidence. By growth and metabolism, the germ had been grouped with fast-growing relatives.

Multiple lines of evidence establish it as a distinct species, the authors conclude. Correct naming matters for medicine, since this organism is given to patients. It also matters for comparing research across labs. The study closes a classification debate with a broad evidence base.
plos-pone-0006363:
The tips of chromosomes hold repeat blocks whose names and counts shift from tip to tip. Xuefeng Zhu and Claes Gustafsson mapped the packing of DNA at two such blocks in baker's yeast for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. All yeast tips share the same kind of end repeats, but the blocks next to them vary in place and count.

The two block types, called X and Y prime, proved to have sharply unlike packing. Packing decides which genes near the tip are on or off. Genome wide maps let the team see the split at every tip at once. The work shows that like DNA can be packed in unlike ways, with real effects on the cell.
plos-pone-0006463:
Derek Alsop, Jennifer Ings, and Mathilakath Vijayan studied stress and breeding in zebrafish for PLOS ONE in 2009. Stress is known to harm reproductive performance, but the pathways are not fully mapped. Hormones of the stress system act on the brain-pituitary-gonad axis, the chain that controls reproduction. One key stress hormone in that chain is ACTH.

Their title reports that ACTH suppresses estradiol release from zebrafish ovarian follicles when gonadotropins stimulate them. Estradiol is a key egg-related hormone. A direct brake at the ovary helps explain how stress cuts fertility. The fish model gives a clean way to trace those effects.
plos-pone-0006563:
Stephanie Wai, Scott Gerber, and Rong Li studied repeated marking of a yeast polarity factor in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cell polarization is essential for processes such as cell migration and asymmetric cell division. A common regulator of polarization in most eukaryotic cells is the conserved Cdc42 protein. In yeast, its exchange factor is Cdc24.

The team examined multisite phosphorylation of Cdc24 during yeast cell polarization. Many phosphate tags, rather than one switch, tune the factor's behavior. Multisite control allows graded, robust responses. Yeast polarization is a model for how all cells pick a front and back.
plos-pone-0006663:
Alice van Gemert and co-authors watched RNA move inside living fly muscle cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. In skeletal muscle, each muscle cell, commonly called a myofiber, is actually a large syncytium containing numerous nuclei. Experiments in fixed myofibers show mRNAs remain near their nucleus of origin. The team monitored mRNA movement in vivo in Drosophila body wall muscle cells.

Their title reports the presence of myofiber domains: each nucleus governs its local territory. Local control lets a giant cell vary protein production by region. Watching it live confirms what fixed tissue suggested. The finding shapes models of muscle disease, where domains break down.
plos-pone-0006763:
Ben Adams and Durrell D. Kapan modeled how human travel spreads mosquito-borne disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. City people travel often and widely. Much of that travel follows structured commuting patterns. Mosquitoes bite locally, but people carry infections between neighborhoods. The authors asked how commuting shapes disease dynamics. Dengue is their motivating example of a vector-borne pathogen.

Their analysis used a metapopulation model of connected patches. Movement data linked the patches as commuters do daily. The model shows human movement can dominate spread patterns. Mosquito control alone may miss the human half of transmission. The work gives city health planners a more realistic spread picture.
plos-pone-0006863:
Ignacio J. Gomez Portillo and Pablo M. Gleiser modeled brain networks that rewire themselves in PLOS ONE in 2009. Brain functional networks map regions as nodes and coordination as links. These networks show a robust small-world structure. They also contain highly integrated modules. A static model cannot capture how connections adapt.

Their adaptive complex network model lets links change with activity. Adaptation rules generate the small-world, modular pattern naturally. Such models help explain how brain organization emerges and stays flexible. They also provide test beds for ideas about learning. The work bridges network theory and neuroscience in a compact model.
plos-pone-0006963:
Grégory Lacraz, Marie-Hélène Giroix, Nadim Kassis, and colleagues tested a diabetes treatment in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. In type 2 diabetes, the insulin-making islets of the pancreas become inflamed and scarred. That inflammation may start in the islets' own blood vessel lining. The team studied islets from GK rats, a diabetic strain.

They measured genes tied to vessel activation and oxidative stress. Then they gave a treatment called IL-1Ra and measured again. Gene expression for activation and stress went down with treatment. The result supports calming islet inflammation as a way to protect insulin output.
plos-pone-0007063:
Bédis Dridi, Mireille Henry, Amel El Khéchine, and colleagues improved gut microbe detection in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two methane-making archaea live in the human gut. Methanobrevibacter smithii and Methanosphaera stadtmanae help drive digestion. Yet tests found their DNA in stool at low and variable rates. The team blamed weak detection methods for the mismatch.

With an improved DNA protocol, they found both microbes at high prevalence. The earlier scarcity was a measurement problem, not a biological one. Reliable detection matters because these archaea affect gut gas, digestion, and possibly disease.
plos-pone-0007163: Myong-Hee Sung, Luigi Salvatore, Rossana De Lorenzi, and colleagues studied sustained oscillations of NF-κB in PLOS ONE in 2009. NF-κB is a transcription factor that rises and falls in waves inside cells. Their work showed that these sustained waves produce distinct patterns of genome scanning and gene expression. In other words, the rhythm itself carries information. The timing of the signal, not just its strength, helps decide which genes a cell switches on.
plos-pone-0007263:
Eric Fimbel, Stéphane Lauzon, and Constant Rainville compared humans with computer algorithms on a planning test in 2009. The Tower of London test assesses executive functions such as planning. It was inspired by artificial intelligence tasks originally built to test problem-solving algorithms in machines.

The authors compare human performance with exploration algorithms on the same test. They focus on search patterns rather than absolute execution times. Their PLOS ONE comparison shows where human planning matches machine search and where it differs. Psychologists can use the benchmark to judge both patients and algorithms more fairly.
plos-pone-0007363:
Pontus Nordenfelt, Susanne Bauer, Per Lönnbro, and colleagues reassessed a cell model for studying bacterial killing in 2009. HL-60 cells treated with retinoic acid become neutrophil-like. Neutrophils are white blood cells that engulf and kill bacteria, and HL-60 cells carry the same azurophilic granules that store killing compounds.

New approaches to the neutrophil phagosome prompted a fresh look at this model. The authors study phagocytosis of Streptococcus pyogenes by the differentiated cells. They examine roles of azurophilic granules and the enzyme NADPH oxidase. Their work tests how faithfully the model mimics real neutrophils.
plos-pone-0007463:
Soledad Sacristán and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on powdery mildew fungi, parasites that infect nearly ten thousand plant groups. These fungi live entirely on their hosts and constantly overcome plant defenses. How they adapt so fast at the molecular level was poorly understood. The team studied a family of their virulence effectors, the proteins used to attack hosts.

They found these effectors evolve in step with LINE-1 retrotransposons, mobile pieces of DNA often called jumping genes. That coevolution suggests the jumping genes help shuffle or spread the attack proteins. A parasite that can reinvent its weapons quickly is hard for plants to resist. The finding offers a mechanism behind the mildew's speed. It may also guide efforts to breed more durable crop resistance.
plos-pone-0007563:
Tamim Salehzada and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how muscle cells choose their fate. Building and repairing skeletal muscle takes several coordinated steps. Stem cells wake, multiply, then mature into muscle fibers. Hundreds of genes switch on and off along the way. The team studied an enzyme called RNase L, which cuts RNA, and its influence on that choice.

RNase L regulates the myogenic and adipogenic potential of the cells. In plain terms, it helps decide whether they become muscle or fat. An RNA-cutting enzyme in that role shows how much control sits after genes are read. The balance between muscle and fat matters in aging and disease. The study adds a new switch to the known controls of muscle maintenance and repair.
plos-pone-0007663:
Jinte Middeldorp and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a variant protein in the brain's support cells. Astrocytes make GFAP, a structural protein with several splice variants. Two variants produce a form with a shifted tail, detectable by an antibody called GFAP+1. That form had been reported in astrocytes and in degenerating neurons in Alzheimer's disease. The team used an affinity-purified version of the antibody to test the claims cleanly.

The purified antibody revealed a specific astrocyte subtype carrying the variant. Unpurified serum, by contrast, cross-reacted with a neuronal protein in Alzheimer samples. That cross-reaction could mislead anyone reading such stains. The paper is both a discovery and a caution. A cleaner tool finds a real subtype, while the dirty tool invents a false one. Dementia research, which leans on GFAP stains, needs exactly that distinction.
plos-pone-0007763:
Kunihiro Kishida and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests whether a DNA variant in mitochondria relates to temperament. Mitochondria are the cell's energy centers, with their own small genome. One variant, A10398G, had been linked to mental disorders such as bipolar disorder.

The team studied healthy young adults in Japan. Healthy volunteers let researchers see gene effects without illness in the way. They measured temperament traits and compared them across variant groups. If such links hold, small energy-gene differences might nudge personality. The study treats that idea with proper caution.
plos-pone-0007863:
Cyndi Chen and Chih-Pin Liu published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It describes a new kind of regulatory T cell in mice. Regulatory T cells keep the immune system from attacking the body. Most known types carry the marker Foxp3, but this population does not.

The cells are specific to a mouse autoantigen, a self molecule. Their regulatory function depends on three things. They need the signal IFN-gamma, the gas nitric oxide, and direct contact with target cells. Antigen-specific regulators are more potent than general ones. This new group may offer a precise tool against autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0007963:
Kareem Elsayad and Katrin Heinze set the working rules for a metal film lens in PLOS ONE in 2009. Thin metal films can bend light in ways that beat the usual limit on fine detail. That trick, called a superlens, could image glowing molecules with rare sharpness.

The pair worked out when the lens truly works for such imaging and when it fails. Clear rules matter because near-field lenses are touchy; small shifts in setup can spoil the gain. Their bounds help builders design setups that gain real sharpness rather than chasing a mirage.
plos-pone-0008063:
Andrew Shepherd and colleagues found a new control on the Notch signal in fly embryos for PLOS ONE in 2009. Notch steers the fate of cells in nearly every tissue as an animal grows. Most known controls act on the Notch protein after it is built.

This control acts earlier, on the cutting and finishing of the Notch message RNA. Holding the message back lowers how much protein the cell can make. An early brake like this adds fine timing to a signal whose doses must be exact for organs to form rightly.
plos-pone-0008163:
Nicole Nasby-Lucas and colleagues followed white sharks into their open ocean months in PLOS ONE in 2009. White sharks are well watched near coasts, but in the eastern Pacific they vanish offshore for up to five months. Tags that record depth, light, and place let the team follow that hidden season.

The sharks shared a broad offshore feeding ground and used its waters in set ways, diving and cruising in patterns tied to its conditions. The first full portrait of that season fills a blank in the species' life. It also tells protectors which waters matter most.
plos-pone-0008263:
Katja Linher, Paul Dyce, and Julang Li grew germ-like cells in the lab in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Stem cells from fetal pig skin had earlier formed oocyte-like cells in culture. Oocytes are the egg cells of reproduction. Before eggs can form, primordial germ cells must be specified. Those are the early cells set aside to become sperm or eggs.

The team showed skin-derived stem cells could produce primordial germ cell-like cells in vitro. That step bridges skin stem cells and later egg-like cells. The work matters for fertility research and animal breeding. It also probes how cell identity can be redirected.
plos-pone-0008363:
Caren I. Lanting and colleagues studied pregnant smokers in the Netherlands in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Smoking is a major cause of illness and death, including during pregnancy. Effective ways to promote quitting in pregnancy exist. Their national impact, though, had not been studied. The team estimated how common smoking in pregnancy is and which risks cluster around it.

Socioeconomic, behavioural, and neonatal risk factors clustered in pregnant smokers. Clustered risks mean smoking mothers often face several disadvantages at once. Support programs must therefore address more than cigarettes alone. The findings guide national maternal health policy.
plos-pone-0008463:
Nathan Jorgensen and co-authors test a part of the LRRK2 protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Changes in LRRK2 are the most common gene cause of Parkinson disease. The protein has a core with enzyme parts. It also has parts that bind other proteins. One binding part is the WD40 domain. The team ask if that part is needed for harm to nerve cells.

They find that without the WD40 domain, LRRK2 loses its toxic effect. That shows the domain is required for neurotoxicity in their model. The result points drug work at that part of the protein. Blocking its contacts may protect nerve cells.
plos-pone-0008563:
Wenyan Chen and co-authors study calcium sensing at nerve terminals in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When a spike invades a nerve terminal, it opens voltage-gated channels. Calcium entry then triggers vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release. Ion channels shape the presynaptic spike and thus regulate calcium signals. External calcium outside the terminal also carries information. The team test if the calcium-sensing receptor detects that external signal in neocortical terminals.

They find presynaptic external calcium signaling involves that receptor. The receptor lets terminals sense calcium levels around them. That sensing can adjust release strength in a feedback loop. The work adds a sensor to the standard picture of synaptic transmission.
plos-pone-0008663:
Claudia Nold-Petry and co-authors study a rare immune disease in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Familial hemophagocytosis, or FHL, is associated with defects in CD8 T cell cytotoxicity proteins. Hyperactivation of immune cells results in a perilous, Th1-driven cytokine storm. The team explore regulation of cytokines in an FHL patient. They focus on interleukin 18 binding protein, an anti-inflammatory decoy. Interferon gamma normally induces that binding protein to brake inflammation.

They find interferon gamma fails to induce it in familial hemophagocytosis. Without that brake, IL-18 driven inflammation runs unchecked. The failure helps explain the lethal cytokine storm of FHL. Restoring the brake could be a therapeutic goal.
plos-pone-0008763:
Deepak Lamba, Andrew McUsic, Roli Hirata, and colleagues grew replacement eye cells from reprogrammed human cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Photoreceptors are the light-sensing cells lost in many blinding diseases. Replacing them could restore some vision. Induced pluripotent stem cells can become almost any cell type. Turning them into clean photoreceptors was the challenge.

The team developed steps to derive and purify photoreceptors. They then transplanted the cells to test survival and placement. A reliable source of new retinal cells is the base for future therapy. The recipe moves cell replacement for blindness closer to practice.
plos-pone-0008863:
Shaohui Liu, Jinfang Ma, Wei Wang, and colleagues broke single building blocks of a virus enzyme to find the ones it cannot lose. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, phiC31 integrase, swaps DNA segments with high precision. Gene engineers use it to insert DNA at chosen addresses. Parts of the enzyme outside its known working core are highly conserved. Their roles had never been tested systematically.

Mutating those conserved residues revealed several that are essential. Without them, DNA recombination failed. Knowing the essential parts helps engineers tune the tool safely. It also explains how this enzyme family evolved its precision.
plos-pone-0008963:
Deron Burkepile and Mark Hay asked which plant-eaters a Caribbean reef really needs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Algae can smother coral if grazing fish and urchins disappear. Grazers keep seaweed down and give young coral room to grow. But reefs host many kinds of grazers, and they may not all matter equally.

The pair ran experiments separating the effects of different herbivores on the reef. Which grazer was present changed how algae took over and how coral grew. Losing one key species hurt more than losing another. Reef managers can use that ranking to protect the grazers that count most.
plos-pone-0009063:
Amit Pandey, Neha Munjal, and Malabika Datta asked what an inflammation signal makes liver cells do, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The signal, TNF-alpha, helps decide whether liver cells live or die. It also drives disease in several liver conditions. The test bed was HepG2, a standard human liver cell line.

Gene profiling plus network analysis mapped the cells' full response. Genes for fat and steroid handling stood out as the most favoured group. That bias was stronger than the classic death or survival programmes. Inflammation in the liver may reshape metabolism first and foremost.
plos-pone-0009163:
Yongguang Tao and co-authors caught gene silencing in the act of stalling the copying machine, in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA methylation is a chemical tag that silences genes. Developmental genes are often shut this way once their work ends. How methylation stops transcription at single genes was murky.

The protein Lsh helped stall RNA polymerase II mid-gene. At HoxC6 and HoxC8, the machine paused instead of being blocked at the start. That stalling involved methylation of the surrounding DNA. Silencing, it turns out, can ambush a gene already being read.
plos-pone-0009263:
Hezhao Ji and co-authors published this HIV testing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Health agencies watch for HIV that is already drug-resistant when transmitted. Standard surveillance genotypes each patient's virus one sample at a time. That is slow and costly when hundreds of samples must be checked.

The team used pyrosequencing, a method that reads many samples in parallel. They pooled specimens and sequenced them together to hunt for resistance mutations. Pooling keeps the key information while cutting the workload sharply. If the approach holds up, resistance surveillance could cover far more people for the same money.
plos-pone-0009363:
Todd Edwards and co-authors published this statistics paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diseases often arise from genes interacting, not from single genes alone. A search method called MDR hunts through combinations of genes for joint effects. After such an exhaustive search, researchers need a formal test that an interaction is real.

The authors present a general framework for that testing step. They apply it to MDR and its paired variant, MDR-PDT. A proper test guards against patterns that look strong but arise by chance. The framework strengthens genetic studies that claim two or more genes work together.
plos-pone-0009463:
Peter Hauser and co-authors built a delivery trick for kidney cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Podocytes wrap around the kidney's tiny filters. When they are hurt, serious kidney disease can follow. Small RNA pieces, called siRNA, can turn off a chosen gene. Getting those pieces into podocytes inside a living animal is hard.

Podocytes eagerly take in material from their surroundings. The team used that habit to carry siRNA into the cells in mice. The method reached the target cells and lowered the chosen gene's output. It opens a route to test gene based treatments right where much kidney damage starts.
plos-pone-0009563:
Matthew Muller and colleagues tested scoring systems for flu patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flu season brings crowds of patients to hospitals. Doctors need a fast way to judge who is most at risk. Scores built for pneumonia and for general illness are often used. The team checked how well those scores predicted intensive care admission and death in confirmed flu cases.

Good scores would let hospitals send low risk patients home with confidence. They would also flag high risk patients for close care early. The study measures each score against real outcomes. That gives clinicians an evidence based tool for the hardest weeks of the flu season.
plos-pone-0009663:
Akihiro Yamashita, Sandi Nishikawa, and Derrick Rancourt studied stem cell fate in PLOS ONE in 2010. Embryonic stem cells can become many cell types. Guiding them to bone is a goal for repair medicine. The team grew differentiating stem cells in varied surroundings. They asked how the cells' microenvironment steers commitment to the bone lineage, the osteogenic path.

The surroundings clearly modulated whether cells committed to bone. Signals from the neighborhood weighed alongside the cells' own programs. That means growing replacement bone depends on setting the right scene, not just picking the right cells. The work gives tissue engineers a lever they can adjust.
plos-pone-0009863:
The immune system learns self from the small protein pieces shown to it. Cristina Clement and colleagues compared those pieces in human lymph and in blood plasma. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lymph is the fluid that drains tissues and carries immune cells.

A peptidome is the full set of peptides, short protein fragments, in a fluid. Lymph carried an expanded self-antigen peptidome compared with plasma. That means lymph holds a wider range of the body's own pieces. A wider display could shape how immune cells learn tolerance.
plos-pone-0009963:
Thinning ozone lets more ultraviolet light reach the water where fish embryos grow. Ben Wang and colleagues built tiny shells to shield zebrafish embryos from that harm. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ultraviolet light can damage DNA in growing embryos.

Shell engineering means coating each embryo in a protective layer. The strategy aims to guard embryo development from ozone depletion effects. Zebrafish are a standard model for development studies. A working shield could protect farmed and wild fish alike during early life. The shells were built one embryo at a time.
plos-pone-0010063:
The authors were Latha Satish, Sandra Johnson, James Wang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study began with a puzzle about scars. Wounds in unborn mammals heal with no scar at all. Adult wounds, by contrast, contract and leave marks, and the signals behind the difference remain unclear.

The team identified a protein called CCT-eta as a specific regulator in fibroblasts. Fibroblasts are the cells that move into wounds and pull tissue together. Controlling their motion and contraction could, in time, help adult wounds heal more like fetal ones. The study was published in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010163:
The authors were Carmen Maffettone, Guohua Chen, Ignat Drozdov, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined an iron control protein in cancer. Iron regulatory proteins bind RNA messages and control how iron-related proteins are made. One of them, IRP1, seemed to suppress tumors in animal tests, raising interest in its sibling, IRP2.

The team focused on a specific insert of seventy-three amino acids inside IRP2. They linked that insert to tumorigenic properties, meaning the ability to promote tumors. A defined protein segment like that gives drug designers a precise feature to study.
plos-pone-0010263:
The authors were Outi Hovatta, Marisa Jaconi, Virpi Töhönen, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study inspected stem cell lines for dangerous genome changes. One Swiss human embryonic stem cell line showed features of a malignant line. It came from the only cell that survived freezing of an embryo, and resembled teratocarcinoma lines more than normal stem cells.

The team compared that line with four other human embryonic stem cell lines. They found genomic changes that could be oncogenic, able to promote cancer. Screening for such changes is vital before stem cells are used in patients.
plos-pone-0010363:
Jun-Ichi Miyazaki and co-workers traced the family history of deep-sea mussels in PLOS ONE in 2010. These mussels, in the group Bathymodiolus, live where no sunlight reaches. They thrive near vents and seeps by hosting bacteria that make food from chemicals. How such animals first entered the deep sea was a standing puzzle. So was the order in which their lineages spread.

The authors compared genes across mussel species to build an evolutionary tree. The tree suggests paths by which shallow-water ancestors adapted to the depths. Each step demanded tolerance for cold, pressure, and strange chemistry. Knowing that history helps explain today's vent communities. It also frames how life colonizes extreme places more generally.
plos-pone-0010463:
Emmanouil Angelakis and Didier Raoult linked gut bacteria to weight gain in young farm birds in PLOS ONE in 2010. Suspicion had grown that gut microbes help drive obesity. Probiotic foods, which add live bacteria, can shift gut communities. The team checked newborn broiler chicks and ducks as their gut flora formed. They tracked one bacterial group, Lactobacillus, against the birds' growth.

Birds with more of those bacteria in the gut gained more weight. In farming, faster growth is prized, and probiotics are already fed to stock. In human health, the same effect could be unwelcome. The study shows one microbe group's influence in a simple, fast system. It hints that managing gut flora may manage weight, for better or worse.
plos-pone-0010563:
Jian-You Liao and co-workers sequenced small RNAs from both parts of human cells and found a surprisingly complex layout in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators, about twenty-two units long. They were thought to work mainly in the cell's outer body, the cytoplasm. Reports had begun placing some in the nucleus, the cell's control center. The team deep-sequenced small RNAs from each compartment separately.

The two compartments held distinct, intricate mixes of small RNAs. Pieces of transfer RNA also appeared in unexpected places. Location changes what a regulator can reach and control. Maps of where small RNAs live are therefore basic to understanding them. This study redraws that map for human cells.
plos-pone-0010663:
Nicolas Pugeault, Florentin Wörgötter, and Norbert Krüger modeled how vision resolves confusing scenes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early vision is noisy: edges, depths, and surfaces arrive as mixed signals. The brain must settle on one reading of a scene, not several at once.

Their model used feedback between grouping, depth, and shape processes. Grouping cues helped decide which surfaces owned which borders. That decision then cleaned up the depth reading. Models with this kind of feedback match human vision better than one-way pipelines. They also offer designs for robots that have to read cluttered rooms.
plos-pone-0010763:
Michelle Wehling-Henricks and colleagues traced how immune cells worsen scarring in muscular dystrophy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a lethal inherited muscle disease that strikes young boys. Weak muscle is slowly replaced by scar tissue, in limbs and heart alike. Steroids are nearly the only treatment.

In mdx mice, the standard model, macrophages processed the amino acid arginine in a way that fed scarring. Blocking that route reduced fibrosis in muscle and heart. The immune system is thus a driver of scarring, not a bystander. A drug aimed at that route could complement future gene therapies.
plos-pone-0010863:
Maria Leonor Oliveira, Eliane Miyaji, Daniela Ferreira and co-authors published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of deadly lung and blood infections in young children, especially in poorer countries. The authors tested a vaccine built around PspA, a surface protein of the bacterium, boosted by an unlikely helper.

Their helper was the whole-cell pertussis vaccine already given to children in the combined diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis shot. Mice given PspA through the nose together with that vaccine were better protected against a pneumococcal challenge than mice given the protein alone. Oliveira and colleagues argue that a cheap, familiar vaccine can double as an adjuvant. That could lower the cost of protecting children where pneumococcal disease hits hardest.
plos-pone-0010963:
Rikard Fristedt, Pontus Granath and Alexander Vener published this plant study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inside plant chloroplasts, the membranes where photosynthesis happens stack into piles, and adding phosphate tags to photosystem proteins influences that stacking. The authors asked how much tagging is enough to change the membrane architecture.

Using light-scattering measurements on membranes from the model plant Arabidopsis and mutants missing specific tagging enzymes, they showed stacking responds strongly to magnesium levels and to which tags are present. Mutants unable to tag one photosystem part stacked their membranes even without magnesium, while extra tagging under strong light increased magnesium dependence. Fristedt and colleagues identify a phosphorylation threshold for membrane organization. The result links a molecular switch to the physical layout that lets plants tune light capture.
plos-pone-0011063:
Qing-He Zhang and Fredrik Schlyter published this insect chemical ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Predatory beetles find their bark beetle prey by smelling kairomones, chemical cues leaking from the prey's world. The authors hypothesized that odors from plants the prey never touches could jam that tracking, an off-pathway signal they call a bypass-trophic cue.

Working with a predaceous clerid beetle, they confirmed by antenna recordings that it detects several volatiles from broadleaf plants, its prey's non-hosts. Two mushroom-like alcohols, 3-octanol and 1-octen-3-ol, were especially active on the antenna. Zhang and Schlyter show a predator's nose pays attention to smells from outside its food chain. Such jamming signals could be used in forestry to protect trees, by hiding prey from its enemies or pests from theirs.
plos-pone-0011163:
Domitrovic, Kozlov, Freire and colleagues characterized a yeast protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. Yeast is among the most studied organisms on Earth, yet this protein had no known role. Through structure and function tests, the team linked it to control of metabolism and to drug resistance.

Filling such a gap shows how much basic biology remains hidden in familiar genomes. A protein that affects drug resistance could matter for fighting fungal infections. It may also reveal shared control circuits in other cells. The careful study of one unknown protein thus widens several fields at once.
plos-pone-0011263:
Thibodeaux, Liang, Moncivais and colleagues rewired mammal cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. A matched pair of molecules from archaea can add new building blocks to proteins without disturbing the host's own system. The team adapted that pair, used for rewriting the genetic code, to function inside mammalian cells.

With the pair working, custom proteins carrying new chemistry become possible in mammal systems. Such proteins can test how small chemical changes alter function. They may also lead to medicines with properties nature never evolved. The study hands synthetic biology a tool previously limited to simpler cells.
plos-pone-0011363:
Elodie Monsellier and colleagues used computer models in 2010 to study how sugar chains speed up harmful protein clumping. In diseases such as Alzheimer's, proteins gather into stiff fibers called amyloid, and long sugar chains found between cells can make that gathering much faster. Testing each sugar variant in the lab is slow, so the team modeled the chemistry instead.

Their models sorted which chemical traits of the sugar chains drive the speed-up, separating key features from minor ones. That ranking tells chemists what to block if they want to slow fiber growth. It also shows how modeling can narrow a wide field of suspects before costly lab work begins. For amyloid research, the paper offers both a method and a short list of chemical factors most worth targeting next.
plos-pone-0011463:
Colleen Manitt and co-authors found in 2010 that rodent dopamine neurons switch on a guidance receptor right around puberty. Dopamine circuits are heavily remodeled in adolescence, and miswiring in that window is linked to mental illness. The receptor, UNC-5, helps steer growing nerve fibers by telling them where not to go, yet it was barely present in these neurons before puberty.

Its emergence at peri-puberty suggests adolescence opens a defined window when guidance cues redirect dopamine wiring. Events in that window, from stress to drugs, may have outsized effects because the steering system has just come online. The timing gives developmental neuroscience a concrete target: a receptor, a cell type, and a life stage. It may help explain why the teenage brain is at once so adaptable and so vulnerable.
plos-pone-0011563:
Ashley Bear and co-authors took a three-sided portrait in 2010 of a butterfly mutation that darkens the caterpillar. The butterfly Bicyclus anynana is a laboratory favorite famous for seasonal forms, wearing different wing patterns in wet and dry seasons. A mutant with a dark larval cuticle offered a window into how one genetic change ripples through a whole animal.

The team characterized the mutation genetically, morphologically, and physiologically: where it sits, what it does to the body, and how it changes the animal's inner workings. Few mutations get all three readings, and each alone would mislead. Together they show how a single change can be a pigmentation story, a development story, and a physiology story at once. Such complete portraits teach geneticists how much of an animal one gene can reach.
plos-pone-0011663:
Erik Schlicht and co-authors ran betting experiments to test the power of first impressions, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Research on competitive games usually assumes players judge opponents from past results and cold calculation. Far less was known about how a quick look at an opponent's face shapes decisions in the moment.

Schlicht's team found that human wagering shifts with the opponent's face, even before any track record exists. Rapid social impressions leak into choices that textbook models treat as pure maths. The result matters for economics and game design, since real competitors always bring faces, not just pay-off tables.
plos-pone-0011763:
Fabio Morandi and co-authors described a new way a tolerance protein disarms T cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Soluble HLA-G has many immune-calming functions, helping explain how a mother tolerates her baby. Efficient immune responses depend on chemotaxis, the directed travel of immune cells toward chemical signals, which requires working chemokine receptors.

The team showed soluble HLA-G lowers chemokine receptor expression on human T cells and impairs their travel for the first time. A protein that grounds the immune system's patrols could be exploited by tumours, and blocking it might restore immune movement.
plos-pone-0011863:
Andrew Scott and colleagues studied in 2010 how blood vessels stay stable while the retina develops its circulation. VEGF, the vessel growth signal, is made strongly by astrocytes, star-shaped support cells in areas the vessels have not yet reached. It is also made by astrocytes inside zones where vessels already run.

Focusing on that second source, the work shows astrocyte-made VEGF helping to steady new vessels rather than only calling for more growth. A signal known for starting vessels thus also protects them once built. That dual role matters for eye diseases of early infancy and diabetes, where fragile retinal vessels either grow wrongly or break down.
plos-pone-0011963:
Hong Chen and colleagues compared in 2010 five ways to extract DNA from the western corn rootworm, a beetle whose larvae devastate corn roots. Nearly every molecular study of the pest starts with extraction, and methods differ in yield, cost, and how much they damage the DNA. Commercial kits compete with older bench recipes.

Putting five methods through the same tests gives rootworm researchers a practical ranking for their own work. Cheap, reliable extraction is unglamorous but decisive: population studies of resistance and spread need hundreds of beetles processed the same way. A shared standard method also makes results from different labs easier to compare.
plos-pone-0012063:
Izhar Wallach, Navdeep Jaitly, and Ryan Lilien built in 2010 a method to connect drug side effects back to the biology that causes them. Adverse drug reactions are complex, unwanted effects that follow from taking a medicine. A dominant factor behind many is the drug's ability to disturb particular biological pathways.

Their structure-based approach maps side effects to perturbations of underlying pathways, starting from the drug's chemical structure. Predicting which pathway a new compound will disturb could flag its likely side effects before trials. That would not replace testing, but it could steer chemists away from structures whose side-effect profile is written into their shape.
plos-pone-0012163:
Dominik Wiemuth, Shaun Lott, Kevin Ly, and co-authors studied how kidney and airway cells control salt uptake, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A channel in these cells lets sodium in, and its numbers at the surface set how much salt and water the body keeps. One protein tags the channel for removal, while a hormone-driven kinase protects it from that tag.

The team showed the protective kinase must grip the tagging protein's docking arms to do its job. That grip is a small, precise contact in a system that sets blood pressure and airway wetness. Mapping it adds detail to how diseases of salt balance, from high blood pressure to cystic fibrosis, might be treated.
plos-pone-0012263:
Febitha Kandan-Kulangara, Rashmi Shah, El Bachir Affar, and co-authors checked whether gene silencing survives a cell's death throes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Researchers routinely silence genes with RNA interference to study apoptosis, the cell's self-destruct program, assuming the silencing keeps working while the cell dies. The group had already found that permanent silencing can falter during that process, which would corrupt many such experiments.

Here they tested the short-lived, temporary form of silencing under the same conditions. Knowing which silencing method holds up during cell death decides which past results can be trusted and how future ones should be designed. It is unglamorous work that protects a whole field's conclusions.
plos-pone-0012363:
Michael Nicholls, Tobias Loetscher and Maxwell Rademacher tested whether a known attention quirk bends soccer penalty kicks, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. People tend to judge the middle of a line as slightly off center, and the bias flips between near and far space. The authors asked whether goal kickers show the same rightward lean when they aim at a distant goal.

Kickers' shots missed to the right more than chance would predict, matching the far-space bias seen in lab tests. A tiny brain quirk may thus shape real sporting outcomes. Coaches and players who know about the lean could train against it, and the study shows how lab psychology can show up on the field.
plos-pone-0012463:
Morgane Rolland, Jonathan Carlson, Siriphan Manocheewa and colleagues mapped linked amino acid changes in HIV's Gag protein, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The subtype C virus dominates the global epidemic. Host immune pressure, through HLA molecules, forces escape changes in Gag, but escape often costs the virus fitness, and partner changes arise to pay that cost back.

The team charted which changes travel together under HLA pressure. These compensatory pairs show the virus's escape routes and its constraints. Vaccine designers prize constrained spots, because a virus that mutates there cripples itself. Maps like this help choose vaccine targets the virus cannot easily abandon.
plos-pone-0012563:
Tong Zhao, Diane Trinh, Christina Addison and colleagues paired a cholesterol drug with vessel blockers against cancer, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Lovastatin, a statin, blocks building of mevalonate, a hub molecule in cell chemistry. The team had already seen it hinder the epidermal growth factor receptor; here they tested its action on the VEGF receptor pathway that feeds tumors.

Lovastatin inhibited VEGFR and AKT activation, and combined with VEGFR inhibitors it killed cancer cells synergistically. Repurposing a cheap, safe, off-patent drug as a cancer helper is attractive economics. The pairing now needs animal and clinical tests to see if the dish synergy survives the body.
plos-pone-0012663:
Santos, Geraldes, Afonso and co-authors compared ways to test wild boar for tuberculosis. Boar can carry TB and pass it within wild herds, so tracking the disease in wildlife matters for farms and people. Their 2010 study used animals shot by hunters, the main source of samples in the field.

They checked which tests still give sound results on hunter-harvested animals, where samples are rough and delayed. A test that fails in the field is useless, however good it is in the lab. Their comparison guides disease watches in wild boar across Europe.
plos-pone-0012763:
Hosseini, Sokolow, Vandegrift and co-authors tested how well air travel and social data predict a new pandemic's early path. When a fresh disease emerges, health officials must send scarce help to the right countries fast. Their 2010 study combined flight networks with income and population data to forecast early spread.

They checked whether that mix flags the places a pandemic will reach first. A tool that works in the first confusing weeks could save lives by guiding vaccine and staff placement. The work treats flight maps as public health instruments.
plos-pone-0333563:
Ling Wang, Wanhong Luo, and Yong Liu study how a preschooler's whole day of sleep, sitting, and active play relates to thinking skills. Because the day holds only twenty-four hours, more of one activity means less of another. Their 2026 study fits more than two hundred sixty young children with movement trackers, logs their sleep, and tests skills such as holding back impulses and remembering.

The day's overall mix tied clearly to all three thinking skills tested. More sitting time went with weaker skills across the board, while sleep favored flexible thinking. Swapping a small daily chunk of sitting for sleep nudged scores up in the model. Most other swaps showed no clear effect, so the sleep-for-sitting trade stands out for parents and preschools.
plos-pone-0337863:
Tie studied how budget control links to money results in Russian firms in a 2026 paper. Many firms write budgets but follow them loosely, so it stays unclear whether tight control truly lifts performance. The work drew on public company records and survey answers to build and test a numeric model.

Firms with stronger budget control also showed stronger money results, with a clear positive link between the two. Control helped in part by guiding resources to better uses. Scores for making, carrying out, and reviewing budgets were all fairly high, yet results still rose when control grew tighter, which supports treating budgets as a working tool, not paperwork.
plos-pone-0338763:
Xiaokun Zhao and five colleagues work on clearing dust at the working face of underground mines, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Where a cutting machine chews rock, dust clouds threaten miners' lungs, and the corners on the return air side collect the worst of it under a common push pull ventilation setup. The team modeled airflow in simulation software, then used a structured optimization method to tune the duct settings that shape the air.

Two factors dominated: the angle of the exhaust duct inlet and its diameter. Tuning them cut dust levels at the two worst corners by well over half and by about a third respectively. A quarter scale physical model confirmed the computer results within a few percent. The combined route of simulation, statistical tuning, and bench validation gives mine engineers a repeatable recipe for cleaner air at the face.
plos-pone-0344063:
Natalia Toporikova leads a team of eight probing how a spider's internal clock answers light, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Orb weavers keep flexible daily rhythms yet still lock onto the twenty-four hour day. The researchers gave spiders one hour light pulses at different clock times. They charted how activity cycles shifted, producing a phase response curve. Then they sequenced gene activity in spiders pulsed at the most sensitive hour.

The curve showed unusually large shifts, advances and delays of more than six hours, around a sharp break point in the late subjective night. Many genes switched off within an hour of the pulse, then flipped to higher than normal activity nine hours later. The spider's own clock gene copies also behaved unlike those of other arthropods studied. The work maps both the behavior and the molecular choreography of a very resettable clock.
plos-pone-0344163:
Mebrahtom Birhane Tikue and colleagues compared exclusive breastfeeding among mothers of young infants in rural and urban parts of Ethiopia's Tahtay Maichew district in Tigray. Feeding only breast milk for the first six months is among the strongest protections for babies, yet practice varies. Three hundred forty-six mothers answered structured interviews in the 2023 to 2024 survey.

Rural mothers exclusively breastfed at sixty-eight percent, urban mothers at sixty-four percent, a gap too small to matter, which the authors credit to shared primary health care packages. Education, previous births, and pregnancy check-ups predicted the practice in villages; in town, delivery style and breastfeeding teaching at clinic visits mattered most. Both settings sat slightly above the national average.
plos-pone-0345863:
Ava Mohrazi and Reza Ghasemi-Fasaei work on fertilizer design in this 2026 PLOS ONE agriculture paper. Zinc-poor chalky soils are a worldwide problem that cuts crop yields, and ordinary zinc fertilizer washes through too fast. The pair tested slow-release recipes built from materials such as pectin, biochar, layered minerals, and helpful bacteria.

Using a statistical optimization method, they made twelve candidate fertilizers and modeled which ingredients mattered most. Layered mineral carriers held the most zinc, biochar beat pectin as a base, and combining ingredients boosted zinc content further. Three recipes stood out as most efficient. A fertilizer that meters out zinc slowly could cut waste and cost for farmers on poor soils.
plos-pone-0346163:
Kingston Rajiah and Ellen McLaughlin interviewed fifteen community pharmacists in Northern Ireland about the medicines patients return unused and what happens to them. Returned drugs must legally be destroyed, even when sealed and in date, and pharmacists sit at the point where that waste becomes visible. Conversations ran for about half an hour each and were analysed for recurring themes.

Seven themes emerged, from uneven public awareness of return services to the frustration of destroying usable medicine. Pharmacists described quietly cutting waste by supplying less, teaming informally with doctors and care homes, and carrying the cost of disposal work with little training or guidance. Strict safety rules clash with the wish to reuse, they said. The authors call for clearer policy that protects patients while wasting less.
plos-pone-0346563:
José Carlos Hernández and colleagues draw on twenty-five years of fish surveys around El Hierro in the Canary Islands for this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. In October 2011 an underwater volcano erupted off the island, sending a sulphurous plume across a marine reserve where fishing rules differ by zone.

Fish in the strict no-take zone lost less mass at first and rebuilt faster than fish in less protected waters. Even so, eight years on, no zone had fully returned to its pre-eruption state. Fast-growing parrotfish bounced back quickly, while long-lived groupers stayed below their old levels. Protection, the authors conclude, buys resilience but not a fast reset after a rare disaster.
plos-pone-0347763:
Silvana Maldonado and her team used a vast US surgery file to weigh two ways to fix hard belly hernias. The fix shifts belly muscles to close a large gap. One way is open surgery. The other uses a robot. The team matched like patients across more than five thousand cases. They then tracked harm in the first month, days in bed, and returns to care.

The robot way won by a lot. Harm struck under five per cent, next to near twenty for open work. Wound, surgery, and health harms all fell. Robot patients went home in a day or so, not four. They also came back less. Long-term checks come next.
plos-pone-0347863:
Daniel Groß and colleagues dug through seventeen excavations around Syltholm Fjord in Denmark to reconstruct more than three thousand years of fishing, from late hunter-gatherer times to the Bronze Age. Coastal villages there built stationary wooden fish traps in the shallow lagoon for millennia. Animal bones from the sites trace what people ate and how the fjord's wildlife changed under that steady pressure.

The main fish species stayed constant across the whole span, even as land animals shifted and wild game rose around five thousand years ago when trap use declined. Overall species richness fell steadily toward the Bronze Age, suggesting a simpler ecosystem under heavier human shaping. Diets kept favouring water foods chosen for good returns. The authors reject a sudden farming takeover, describing instead a long mosaic of wild resources.
plos-pone-0347963:
Xuan Liu and colleagues built a gentler mouse model of womb lining scarring, a cause of infertility where the womb lining sticks and thins after injury. Forty mice were split into four groups: ultrasound guided injury through the vagina, open surgery injury, alcohol injury, and open surgery controls. Wombs were checked two weeks later for lining shape, gland counts, and scar tissue.

All three injury methods produced scarring with lost glands and heavy fibrosis versus controls. The ultrasound guided vaginal route caused the fewest early and late complications and avoided belly surgery. A cleaner model helps test scar preventing gels and cell therapies before human trials.
plos-pone-0348363:
Fei Shang, Kosha Dholakia, and Jesse Schallek asked whether a year of high blood sugar visibly remodels the tiny blood vessels of the retina in a widely used diabetic mouse. This mouse strain models type 1 diabetes and is often used to study diabetic eye disease, a leading cause of blindness. Their 2026 study examined retinal tissue from diabetic and healthy mice across ages and also imaged one living diabetic mouse repeatedly over twelve weeks.

Across vessel density, branching, length, waviness, support cell coverage, and connections between vessel layers, the diabetic retinas looked essentially normal. The living mouse likewise showed no change over time and matched the tissue data. The authors conclude that sustained high blood sugar alone, at least in this strain, does not produce the retinal vessel pattern changes researchers can detect with current imaging.
plos-pone-0348463:
Rodolfo Farlora and co-authors tested how neem extract, a plant-based pesticide, affects brine shrimp that were never its target. Neem products are spreading in farming and fish research, yet non-target aquatic effects were thinly documented. Their 2026 study combined survival counts, body checks, gene sequencing, and tissue examination in the shrimp.

Juvenile shrimp died and developed abnormally in a clear dose-dependent pattern. Adult males died more readily than females under longer exposure. Gene data showed juveniles switching off detox and shell-building genes while switching on immune and cuticle programmes. Adults showed stress signatures, including heat shock proteins. Farlora and colleagues warn that natural origin does not make a pesticide harmless to aquatic life.
plos-pone-0348763:
Vesna V. Stevanovic and co-workers test a calming drug given by mist inhaler before children's throat surgery. The drug is used to ease anxiety and pain around operations, and may also blunt body stress. Their 2026 pilot trial randomly assigns children facing tonsil and adenoid removal to the drug or no such pre-treatment, then tracks sedation, pain, and blood markers of stress and swelling.

Thirty-one children took part, split nearly evenly between the groups, with no clear differences in age or surgery length. The abstract reports the setup and early course in detail rather than final verdicts. As a pilot, the study mainly checks that a bigger trial can run cleanly and shows which measures respond.
plos-pone-0348863:
Nayab Asim and co-authors compared image networks and a transformer model for naming chest cancers from scans in 2026. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, and computer help with early, accurate reading is in high demand.

All models were fed images prepared the same tensor based way, using a public annotated data set. Classic networks including ResNet and EfficientNet reached the highest accuracy, while the transformer proved strong at grasping broad image patterns. The side by side test, on equal footing, helps hospitals judge which style of model deserves their computing budget and trust.
plos-pone-0349563:
Long-term hepatitis B clusters in immigrant and poorer communities. This pattern holds across the United States. Grace Dickel and colleagues asked whether neighborhood hardship tracks with infection. They used health records from Washington State. The years covered were 2018 to 2023. Their paper appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Confirmed cases were matched with similar patients. The comparison patients had routine blood tests on record. That gave everyone a fair chance of detection. Home addresses became deprivation scores for small census areas. Finer scoring bands captured the pattern better. Coarse bands blurred it. The authors suggest place-based screening. Vaccination drives could target the hardest-hit blocks.
plos-pone-0349663:
