Fumiya Miyako, Hiroki Ota, and co-authors checked how often surgical instruments pick up bacteria during a common keyhole eye operation that repairs the retina through tiny ports. Infection inside the eye after this surgery is rare but can blind. Their 2026 review covered ninety-six eyes operated on over one winter at their institution, culturing instruments after each case.

Bacteria turned up in about seven percent of cases, on the entry port, the light probe, and a beveled instrument. No patient developed an eye infection during two months of follow-up. Patients who had received antibacterial eye drops before surgery showed a significantly lower contamination risk. The authors warn that contamination happens even with full standard precautions, and they credit the drops with meaningful protection.
plos-pone-0349763:
Spang and Baudin, in a 2026 study, ask how dementia care homes can protect residents' cultural identity as populations grow more diverse. Drawing on a framework that matches a person to their environment, the authors gathered views from care workers and managers. They asked about both the physical setting and the social life of long-term care homes.

Rooms, gardens, food smells, and sounds all carry culture, and so do language, activities, friendships, and rituals. Staff described using these levers to keep residents rooted in who they are. They also named the tensions: safety rules, thin budgets, and uneven cultural skill among staff can crowd out cultural care. The authors call for interpreter services, structured training in cultural competence, and sensory approaches, such as familiar music and scents, that reach residents even as memory and language fade.
plos-pone-0349863:
Aliénor Delsart and co-authors tested a way to measure pain wind-up in dogs in 2026, adapting a validated cat method. Wind-up, where repeated touches hurt more each time, signals a sensitised nervous system and is suspected in dogs with osteoarthritis.

Healthy dogs and dogs with joint disease took repeated light pressure at the foreleg or tail base under several settings. Pain thresholds before and after, plus a conditioning test, sorted dogs into profiles that amplify or damp pain. Some settings proved more reliable than others. A workable dog test opens study of pain processing in a species that hides pain well.
plos-pone-0350163:
Fengling Tan and colleagues simulated what happens when extra weight is placed on top of a slope held in place by soil nails, long rods driven into the ground. Slopes like these support roads and buildings, yet their failure under added load is poorly understood at the level of single grains. The team used a particle-based computer method to watch failure unfold.

Added load steadily lowered the safety margin and deformed the slope. A narrow point load caused local damage, while a wider strip load cut stability sharply up to a certain width and then leveled off. Inside the soil, grains rotated more and stress grew uneven, signs that failure builds grain by grain.
plos-pone-0350263:
Wei Yoon Poh and Fatiha Hana Shabaruddin led a cost study of liver checks in Malaysia. The patients had type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. The goal was to find bad liver scarring early. World guides suggest a blood score first, then a scan. But most clinics in Malaysia lack the scan machines. The team modeled three paths on a group of one thousand patients.

A new path won. It uses the blood score, then a second blood test for borderline cases. It found each case at the lowest cost. It also beat current practice on both cost and yield. The guide-based path found more cases than current practice, but at extra cost. The team backs the two-test path for clinics with no scanners.
plos-pone-0350363:
Freda Haylett and seven colleagues describe this 2026 PLOS One protocol for a pilot trial of a school program meant to prevent sexual violence before it starts. The program runs in Australian secondary schools and includes lessons for Year 9 students, sessions for parents and staff, and student champions who promote the message. Twelve schools take part, with most assigned by chance to run the program or wait.

Because this is a protocol, it lays out a plan rather than results. Students will be surveyed before the program, right after, and six months later about what they know and how they think and intend to act. A parallel qualitative study will examine how the program works and for whom, guiding a possible larger trial.
plos-pone-0350563:
Xiaodong Zhang and colleagues in China published a trial plan in 2026 for keeping the arm artery open after heart procedures done through the wrist. Pressing on the wrist stops bleeding, but too much pressure can close the artery for good. No results are reported yet.

More than eight hundred patients will be split at random between usual hand judged pressure and a balloon system that measures pressure and eases it in steps matched to the body. Ultrasound a day later will check artery closure, alongside bleeding and other problems. Recruitment began in late 2024 at one centre.
plos-pone-0350663:
Ines Levade and colleagues sequenced viruses from archived mosquito pools in Quebec, Canada, species already known as virus carriers. Northern mosquito virus communities are poorly mapped. Gene sequencing sorted the full viral mix in each pool, built family trees for complete genomes, and resolved dozens of full virus sequences.

Sixty virus species appeared, including three that can infect people, many insect only viruses, and several harmless dual host viruses. A new two part virus type from Culex mosquitoes was proposed. Rich hidden diversity in a cold region argues for routine gene based watching, so emerging threats like West Nile virus are spotted before outbreaks.
plos-pone-0350763:
Hospital gardens might help stroke patients move more, meet others, and lift their mood, but nobody knows exactly how. Louisa-Jane Burton and colleagues present a study plan, in PLOS One in 2026, for case studies at three hospitals with different kinds of green space.

Sites include gardens used for therapy, spaces newly designed for stroke survivors, and long-established grounds. The team will map each space, read its design documents, interview designers, and watch how patients actually use the areas across seasons. The goal is to learn how, for whom, and under what conditions gardens aid recovery, so future hospitals can design them deliberately.
plos-pone-0350963:
Who gets to become a skin doctor in the Netherlands, and is that changing? Sheeney T Magdalena and colleagues used national statistics microdata to track the dermatology workforce from 2005 to 2023, in this 2026 PLOS One study of diversity.

Women rose from about a third of dermatologists to well over half. Yet doctors with Turkish, Moroccan, Surinamese, or Caribbean backgrounds stayed underrepresented, and most new entrants still came from Dutch or European families. Parents' social position also mattered in who reached the specialty. The authors say fair access to care starts with a workforce that mirrors the patients it serves.
plos-pone-0351063:
Elif Ilgazi Kilic and Safak Kilic built a learning system to sort cervical cell images for cancer screening. Early sorting saves lives, yet cell differences can be faint and tangled. Their design adds tailored image variation for training, a module that watches cell shape at several scales, and a mixer that reads how each nucleus sits among its neighbours.

On two public image sets the system scored above ninety eight percent correct, topping standard image networks and newer vision transformers. Error rates fell sharply compared with both rivals. Strong scores across cell types and image styles suggest the tool could support busy screening labs, where a second, steady reader helps catch early change.
plos-pone-0351563:
Cheng Tang and Zubing Mei set out a protocol, with no results yet, for pooling research on loss of bowel control after surgery for anal fistula. That loss can damage dignity and social life, and reported rates vary widely by operation and fistula type. Single studies name many possible predictors, yet definitions and adjustments differ across reports.

Under the plan, five sources plus grey literature will be searched without language limits. Only adult cohort or case control studies with clear outcome rules at least three months after surgery will count. Two reviewers will screen, extract, and judge bias with standard tools. Pooling will favour adjusted estimates and probe how fistula difficulty and operation type change risk.
plos-pone-0351763:
Allison Shay and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of heart failure care. It compares heart failure patients who have type 2 diabetes with those who do not. The data come from nineteen years of a nationwide American hospital records system. The records cover nearly one hundred forty thousand heart failure patients. The team compared how often patients were admitted, how long the first stay lasted, and at what age it came. They also split the results by heart failure subtype.

About three in ten patients had diabetes. Those patients were admitted more often. They stayed slightly longer. They arrived for their first stay about a year and a half younger than patients without diabetes. Diabetes was most common in the diastolic subtype. The age gap at first stay was largest there too. The authors say diabetes status and subtype together shape the load hospitals carry.
plos-pone-0351963:
Rachel Lumbis and four colleagues survey first-year veterinary and veterinary nursing students in Britain and Ireland about where they learn pet nutrition, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. More than three hundred students answered. Most were keen to learn about small-animal nutrition, and they rated qualified vets and professional journals as the most trustworthy sources, with social media and friends at the bottom.

Yet barely half felt able to actually find and use evidence-based nutrition information. Students also assumed vets know more about nutrition than nurses do. The authors spot the paradox — the most trusted sources are not always the used ones — and urge educators to teach information-finding skills, not just facts.
plos-pone-0352163:
Eric Ng'eno reexamined what decides which drug-resistant E. coli strains settle in people's guts in a crowded informal settlement in Kenya. Resistant gut bacteria are usually blamed on antibiotic use alone, but these bacteria live in communities of microbes with histories. His analysis weighed drug pressure, which strains were already established, feedback between strains, and how strains spread between people and places.

Different forces ruled different strains. Where bacteria-killing antibiotics were common, long-established local strains dominated. Where gentler, growth-stopping antibiotics were common, newer strains gained ground more easily. Hygiene habits also shaped the mix. The takeaway for public health is that resistance is an ecology problem, not only a prescribing problem: wiping out today's strains without changing the conditions can simply open seats for tomorrow's.
plos-pone-0352263:
Kwak and colleagues built a lab model of the blood-brain barrier during stroke in a 2026 study. When blood flow stops, a ring of partly injured tissue around the dead core may still be saved. The team's chip held human cells in three dimensions and was starved of oxygen and sugar to mimic that border zone.

Restoring flow alone helped the barrier heal, but cooling the cells during restored flow helped most. Cell shape recovered, sealing proteins returned, and a marker of low oxygen fell. Because the model uses human cells, it offers a closer test bed for stroke drugs than animal tissue alone. Future work can screen treatments on the chip before trials.
plos-pone-0352463:
Til Böttner and colleagues checked whether a cheap underwater recorder, the HydroMoth, can report true sound levels on the sea floor, not just relative loudness. Ecologists use such recorders to study reef and seabed life and ship noise, but turning recordings into pressure levels takes calibration. The team tuned nine units against a reference tone and compared them with a factory-calibrated recorder in tank and field tests.

In the low-frequency band that matters for seabed animals and ships, the small recorders stayed close to the reference, usually within a few decibels. Field units matched that accuracy. For research groups priced out of high-end gear, the result is welcome: with careful one-point calibration, a budget recorder can support real measurements of underwater noise rather than rough impressions.
plos-pone-0352663:
Wang, Zhang, and Xu hunted for key genes behind psoriasis in a 2026 study. Psoriasis is a lasting skin condition driven by genes, immunity, and environment acting together. The team combined single-cell gene data from sore and healthy skin with network analysis and machine learning.

Four genes stood out and all ran higher in sore skin than in healthy skin. Hundreds of linked hub genes clustered around sore areas and certain skin cells. The team also screened small drug-like compounds that could target the four genes. Narrowing a crowded gene field to four drivers gives drug researchers clearer targets for the next round of lab testing.
plos-pone-0352763:
Liang Jian Chun leads a team of eight stress testing the plastic that holds brake fluid in cars, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The polypropylene reservoir must never crack or leak. Yet molding and service loads pull it in several directions at once. The team framed crack risk through stress triaxiality, a measure of how hydrostatically a material is pulled apart. They ran flow, tensile, and burst pressure trials on production material.

The plastic behaved robustly. Tensile strength landed in the expected band. The reservoirs burst at a mean pressure nearly four times the required minimum. The authors credit the material's fracture toughness and thermal stability with suppressing crack initiation across the manufacturing conditions they varied. Production deviations still matter, and the paper catalogues them. But the margin between real performance and the safety floor is wide. For a component whose failure means failed brakes, that margin is the story.
plos-pone-0352863:
Thankamani, Biji, and Doss built a learning model to spot drug resistance mutations in tuberculosis bacteria in a 2026 study. Resistant tuberculosis needs different drug mixes, and mutations in distinct genes decide which drugs fail. Their model covers resistance to two key drugs, the combined multi-drug pattern, and a near-extensive pattern.

Training data came from a public patient and genome portal run by United States health institutes. A model that reads mutations directly could speed resistance calls where lab culture is slow. Faster, cheaper resistance profiles help doctors start the right regimen sooner and limit spread of resistant strains.
plos-pone-0352963:
Lan Wei and Jingqi Sun present this 2026 PLOS One computer vision paper on reading handwritten tax receipts automatically. Tax offices handle mountains of messy handwriting, and the authors pair an improved text-spotting network with an improved reading network to find and transcribe receipt text. Their detection stage adds a feature-enhancement module to sharpen its view of faint handwriting.

In testing, the detector located text with high precision and speed, beating two recent rival systems on both counts. The reader likewise transcribed text more accurately and quickly than the comparison methods. The authors present the combined system as a practical way to cut the manual workload of invoice processing while keeping errors low.
plos-pone-0353063:
Azita Rezvani and four colleagues compare two ways of mapping good habitat for the mouflon, a wild sheep, in central Iran, in PLOS ONE in 2026. One model, MaxEnt, learns from where the animals have actually been seen and from environmental data. The other, an ecosystem services toolkit, leans on land cover maps and expert judgment about threats. Running both on the same landscape tests whether they tell the same conservation story.

The sighting based model proved excellent at pinpointing habitat the sheep currently occupy inside protected areas, scoring near the top of standard accuracy measures. The expert based approach brings a different lens, organized around land use and human pressure rather than animal records. Hotspot statistics then marked where suitable ground clusters most strongly. The authors' point is complementarity: one model shows where the species demonstrably thrives today, the other helps judge ground the sheep might need tomorrow.
plos-pone-0353163:
Sagor, Rahman, and Mandal combined standard radio models with machine learning for fifth-generation networks in a 2026 study. Planning such networks needs good guesses of signal strength and speed in cities, villages, and indoor spaces. The team trained five learning methods on ten thousand worked examples built from an official channel guide and real gear details.

Two methods, a neural network and a decision tree, predicted data speed with very high accuracy. Simpler straight-line methods did far worse, which shows how sharply radio behavior bends with place and frequency. Because the training data came from formulas, not field tests, the authors warn that real-world checks still need to follow.
plos-pone-0353363:
Rjoop and colleagues reviewed Hodgkin lymphoma cases at one institution over twenty years in a 2026 study. More than two hundred fifty patients diagnosed between 2002 and 2022 supplied records on symptoms, labs, treatment, and outcomes. The cancer is usually curable, yet some patients resist treatment or relapse.

Median age at diagnosis was twenty-nine, and slightly more than half the patients were men. The most common tissue type was the nodular sclerosis form. Survival analyses searched for early signs that predict worse outcomes. Local outcome data help hospitals in the region set follow-up intensity and counsel patients with realistic figures.
plos-pone-0353463:
Wright and colleagues, in a 2026 exploratory study, compare the microbes in the gut and mouth of people with dyslexia, people with a history of childhood speech apraxia, and their neurotypical relatives. Genes explain only part of these conditions, and the microbiome had barely been checked. Using families as built-in controls is the design's strength, since relatives share homes and much DNA.

Twenty-eight people gave stool and saliva samples, read by gene sequencing. Those with dyslexia stood apart in gut microbe diversity and composition at the species level, a pattern that held across four reference databases and was not seen for speech apraxia. Saliva showed some dyslexia-linked microbes too, but the predicted functional differences appeared only in the gut. With so few participants, the authors stress the work is preliminary: a signal worth a bigger study, not a claim about cause.
plos-pone-0353563:
Alina Savinova and three co-authors probe why tobacco plants make some human medicines well and others barely at all, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Leaves of Nicotiana benthamiana are a popular factory for therapeutic proteins. One test protein, a human immune signal called IL-1, accumulated richly, while a sibling protein, IL-15, could not even be detected in the finished leaf extracts.

Deep protein and chemical profiling showed the two guests pushed the host in opposite directions. The poor producer triggered helper proteins and shut down photosynthesis, while the strong producer steered metabolism toward amino-acid building. Success, it seems, depends on how the guest protein fits the plant's own housekeeping.
plos-pone-0353663:
H. Sridevi, Ramesh Vinayagam, and Raja Selvaraj make a magnetic charcoal from fallen leaves to scrub a common weedkiller from water, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The weedkiller, called 2,4-D, washes off farms into streams. Their material, baked from Tabebuia aurea leaves and laced with magnetic particles, offers a huge internal surface for trapping the chemical — and can be fished out afterwards with a magnet.

Under the best laboratory conditions it removed about four fifths of the weedkiller from test water, and each gram could hold a substantial load. Heat measurements suggested the trapping is physical rather than chemical. After five reuse cycles it still performed well, a practical virtue for cheap water treatment.
plos-pone-0353763:
Sageer and colleagues tested how a farm pesticide harms pangasius fish in a 2026 study. The chemical, thiram, is used to control pests, but wash-off can reach ponds and rivers where fish live. Groups of fish were kept for twelve days in water with low, medium, or higher doses of the chemical.

Fish at higher doses showed more damaged and oddly shaped red blood cells, including extra small nuclei and torn forms. Protective enzymes in the gills and gut fell, while signs of cell stress rose. A DNA damage test also showed more broken genetic material. Together, the results warn that even doses below a quick kill can injure fish over time.
plos-pone-0353863:
Yiming Wang, Ruiqian Qin, and Zhuo Zhang adapt a popular object-detection network to spot blight disease on potato and tomato leaves, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Farm conditions fight back: rain, haze, changing light, and different crops confuse models trained in one setting. Their modified network adds attention modules, style randomisation to harden it against weather, and multi-scale feature mixing, then prunes away nearly half its parameters.

The slimmed model beat the standard version on precision, recall, and detection accuracy, and outperformed several mainstream rivals. A lightweight detector that travels across crops and weather could put early disease warnings into ordinary farmers' hands through a phone camera.
plos-pone-0354163:
Abrahaley Brhane Gebrekidan and three colleagues published this 2026 hospital study of low-birth-weight babies in northern Ethiopia. Records from Suhul Hospital covered more than three hundred newborns admitted between 2021 and 2023. The team used survival curves and risk models to see which babies died in their first weeks and what raised that risk.

Breathing trouble stood out among the dangers the authors flag for action. Their advice centers on things hospitals and families can change: teaching mothers after delivery, starting breastfeeding early, preventing infection, and having oxygen ready. In a conflict-affected region with few resources, such steps offer realistic ways to keep fragile newborns alive.
plos-pone-0354263:
Tasuku Okui examines how marital status shaped deaths in Japan during the COVID-19 pandemic, in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis of national death records from 2010 to 2023. Death rates had been falling for married, single, divorced, and widowed people alike before the pandemic. Okui calculated age-adjusted rates and then compared actual deaths after 2020 with the numbers the earlier trend predicted.

Excess deaths ran highest among people who had never married, especially men, and lowest among the married. Among women the groups were closer, though never-married women under sixty-five clearly fared worse than married peers. The study cannot say why — isolation and weaker support are candidates — but it flags singles as a group pandemic planning overlooks.
plos-pone-0354363:
Luoyuan Cao and colleagues review in 2026 what extra fluid at the back of a fetus's neck on early scans can mean for pregnancy. They looked back at cases at their centre where invasive testing followed the scan finding. Both classic chromosome checks and a finer chip based test were used.

Extra copies of whole chromosomes caused most problems found, above all an extra copy linked to Down syndrome. The finer test also picked up small missing or extra pieces that the classic check missed in babies with normal classic results. Follow-up of uncertain findings was mixed. The authors recommend using both tests together in counselling.
plos-pone-0354463:
Luis Velez-Nandayapa and fellow researchers chart treated glaucoma across the United Kingdom over more than two decades of primary care records. Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and can blind if missed, so health planners need to know how many people are diagnosed and treated. The team counted new and existing treated cases in a huge national database, broken down by age, sex, year, and region.

New case rates held fairly steady through the twenty tens, then dropped sharply in the first pandemic year, likely as routine eye care stalled. Total treated cases kept rising, which the authors link to an aging population. Velez-Nandayapa and colleagues warn that eye services face a growing load even when new diagnoses stay flat.
plos-pone-0354663:
Tanvi Kiran and colleagues set out in 2026 a school trial plan for teenagers in north India whose social media use may harm health and relationships. Schools in three cities will be assigned as whole groups to either a social marketing programme or usual practice. The programme runs for three months and draws on a model of how behaviour changes.

Before and after checks will measure heavy use and linked risks around alcohol, sexual health, and friendships. More than a thousand students are expected across a dozen schools. As a protocol, the work promises a fair test of whether marketing ideas can shift teen habits, not proof that they do.
plos-pone-0354963: Floodwaters chew at riverbanks — and protection measures need numerical testing. This paper numerically investigated structural protection measures against flood flow-driven riverbank damage. The simulations guide engineers toward defenses that hold when rivers rage.
plos-pone-0355163:
Devin Soper, Lauren Cadwallader, and Iain Hrynaszkiewicz reflect in 2026 on how a very large, broad scope journal has tried to support open science at scale. They trace steps such as requiring authors to state where their data can be found, and widening access to protocols, early drafts, and reviews. Figures from the publisher's own open science tracking set show how habits changed over time.

Choice for authors sits at the heart of their account: sharing through added files was allowed where field repositories were lacking. That lowered friction across many fields at once. The authors present the record as a lesson in moving many disciplines toward openness together.
plos-pone-0355463:
Mahmoud El-Awady and co-authors compared ways to estimate equipment lifetimes when tests are stopped early in staged groups. Ending tests early saves time and money, but the missing data complicate reliability estimates. Their 2026 study works with one lifetime distribution and a flexible censoring plan that adapts block by block.

The team derived both classic estimates and Bayesian estimates, the latter built with computer sampling methods. Simulations measured bias, error, interval width, and coverage for each approach. Bayesian estimates came out most accurate, with the narrowest intervals that still covered at the promised rate. Two real examples, cancer survival times and electrical breakdown tests, show how the method shortens testing while keeping key information.
plos-pone-0355563:
Sinéad O'Keeffe and Andrew Lane interviewed teenage Camogie players about playing up into older age grades. Playing up is common in the Irish stick sport, yet the players' own view was missing. Their 2026 study spoke with fifteen adolescent club players who currently play above their age group and analysed the transcripts thematically.

Players described a hard start followed, for most, by real enjoyment. They credited playing up with better skills and stronger social confidence. Costs included heavier pressure, rougher peer moments, and dips in pure fun. Suggested fixes included better social inclusion, backing from coaches and older players, and more player choice. The authors urge developmentally fitting opportunities, not blanket bans or blanket promotion.
plos-pone-0355863:
Aki Ohdera and seven co-authors study regeneration in moon jellyfish in this 2026 paper. These jellyfish do not normally regrow lost appendages, yet earlier work showed that richer feeding can switch that ability on. The team suspected the microbes living on and in the jellyfish might be part of the story, since feeding changes the microbial mix too.

They found that extra nutrients shift the microbiome in a way that reduces a microbe competing with the jellyfish for resources. Antibiotic treatment that copied this shift also promoted regrowth, without any change in diet. Gene activity in the host pointed to a building-block chemical, arginine, and simply adding arginine encouraged appendages to regrow. The results link microbes, diet, and a single nutrient to an animal's power to heal.
plos-pone-0355963:
Rosalio Reyes and Rafael A Barrio built a mathematical model for fighting the New World screwworm. The screwworm is a flesh-eating fly larva. It has returned to Mexico after more than thirty years away. Their 2026 study adapts population equations to the fly's biology. It asks how few sterilized males, released with care, could still wipe the pest out.

Releasing sterile males is the proven weapon against screwworm, but supply is limited. So the model computes release numbers from feedback. It estimates wild fly counts from the infected-animal reports that Mexican authorities already collect. Simulations show eradication in roughly one to two years. Timing is set mostly by the fly's biology. Concentrating releases at the outbreak center and the surrounding region also worked in the spatial version. That guides real control campaigns.
plos-pone-0356063:
Luigi Sacchettino and colleagues compare blood fats in fearful pet dogs against calmer dogs, hunting for a body signature of chronic fear. Fear is the most common behavior problem in family dogs, showing as trembling, hiding, and startle, and it can tip into aggression. Since fats build brain cell walls and carry signals, the team profiled fat species in blood serum from both groups.

Fearful dogs showed a distinct pattern, centered on one family of membrane fats that appeared at altered levels. Other fat classes changed far less. Sacchettino and colleagues read the pattern as a sign that membrane fat handling is disturbed in fearful dogs. They propose the signature as a starting point for lab tests that could support vets treating behavior cases.
plos-pone-0356263:
Victoria Woof and six colleagues ask women from six under-served groups in Britain whether offering breast cancer risk assessment in their thirties and forties would be welcome, in this 2026 study. The proposed service would estimate risk and offer screening or preventive medication to those at higher risk. Fifty-two women joined focus groups and an interview. They included South Asian Muslim, Black, and Roma women, women in poor neighborhoods, women with learning disabilities or autism, and women with long-term anxiety or depression.

Every group was enthusiastic. Women wanted female staff, local venues, a simple process, and privacy promises, plus community events to spread awareness. Many worried about the emotional weight of risk information and wanted clear communication and tailored support. In some communities the disease carried taboo that silenced family discussion. The authors say services built with these communities can narrow early-detection gaps instead of widening them.
plos-pone-0356363:
Mengke Zhu and six colleagues study the soil clinging to highway slopes high in the mountains of western Sichuan, China, in this 2026 paper. Roadside slopes in alpine regions revegetate slowly, and knowing where nutrients sit in the soil guides restoration. The team sieved slope soils by clump size and measured available nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium in each fraction, alongside organic carbon and electrical conductivity, at several elevations.

The largest clumps, over five millimeters, dominated the soil and delivered the biggest share of nutrients. Nutrient levels were relatively high at the two middle elevations sampled, and within each fraction they fell as clump size grew. Organic carbon tracked closely with available phosphorus, and conductivity with all three nutrients. The authors say the results give roadside ecologists a clearer picture of how alpine slope soils store fertility.
plos-pone-0356463:
Doaa Filali and co-authors extend fixed point theory, the branch of mathematics that proves certain equations must have a steady solution. Their setting adds a relation between points, a kind of partial order, and a flexible contraction condition named for earlier researchers, broadened to nearly contractive maps. Working in ordinary distance spaces with a locally well-behaved relation, they prove existence results that swallow many earlier theorems as special cases.

Worked examples in the paper show the new results succeeding where older ones stay silent. As a payoff, the authors apply their theorems to a boundary value problem, proving its solution exists and is unique. The contribution is purely theoretical, aimed at analysts who need sharper tools for differential equations.
plos-pone-0356563:
Afsane Fadaee and a large team revisit the spread of a common sexually spread virus in northeastern Iran, a region shaped by tourism. Doctors sent samples from several thousand people suspected of such infections to regional labs, and the team typed the virus strains found. They then compared the picture with a matching survey done about eight years earlier in the same provinces.

The virus showed up in most samples, most often in adults in their twenties and thirties. Overall share rose by more than a quarter since the earlier survey, and infections carrying many strains at once became far more common. Three of the frequent strains are known cancer-risk types. Fadaee and colleagues say the shift strengthens the case for vaccination and screening in the region.
plos-pone-0356763:
Xin Cao, Aqilah Yaacob, and Kim Mee Chong ran an experiment on China's Xianyu resale platform. They asked whose product photos shoppers find most useful: the seller's own snapshots, polished firm images, or a mix. Their 2026 study showed 660 participants simulated iPhone listings. The design was three-by-two, crossing photo type with higher or lower displayed price. It modeled how information quality and source credibility shaped judged usefulness.

Both quality and credibility fed usefulness. The quality route ran strongest for mixed and firm photos. The credibility route peaked for firm photos alone. Price changed little overall, except that quality mattered more for mixed photos at the higher price. Sellers get a nuanced answer. Professional images build trust, but mixing them with honest user shots carries its own weight.
plos-pone-0357263:
Yanni Ju and colleagues redraw traffic police districts and patrol routes for a real city road network, aiming squarely at resilience when crashes happen. Earlier plans rarely optimized the district map and the routes together. Their two-level model works in stages. An upper level assigns areas to teams. A lower level plans routes. A hybrid of two search algorithms solves it. The goal balances patrol time against fairness of workload between teams.

Against the city's current scheme, the optimized plan cut total weighted patrol time slightly and workload imbalance by a much larger share. Adding teams sped coverage but slowed the solver, and past crash severity proved impossible to ignore in design. Ju and colleagues translate the numbers into practical advice for commanders planning patrol coverage.
plos-pone-0357463:
Jiawei Li and Shengjia Zhang published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE on legal judgment prediction, teaching computers to forecast court outcomes from the written facts of criminal cases. A full prediction has three linked parts: which law articles apply, what the charge is, and how long the penalty runs. Earlier systems ignored the telling keywords in case descriptions, or treated the three parts as independent when they guide each other.

Their model, DTG-KCL, builds a small relationship graph for each case so the subtasks can inform one another case by case. A keyword mechanism, sharpened by contrastive learning, helps the model separate charges that look confusingly alike. On two real legal datasets, the system beat five comparison methods across the subtasks. Their code is released openly, as decision support research showing how structure inside legal tasks can be exploited rather than flattened.
plos-pone-0357763:
Susanne Vogeler, Matthew Parker, Samuel Robson, and Alex Ford wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on small aquatic animals called amphipods. These shrimp-like creatures are widely used in laboratory ecotoxicology, tests of how pollutants affect living things. The authors record their baseline locomotion behavior, how they normally move.

A baseline matters because a chemical's effect can only be judged against what untreated animals do. If normal movement is not well described first, later changes may be missed or misread. Ecotoxicology labs gain a reference for designing cleaner experiments, and the work supports using animal behavior as an early warning of water pollution.
plos-pone-0357963:
Lijun Zhang led a team of five authors building a deep learning tool for lung nodules, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. A nodule on a lung scan poses a dreaded question: harmless, or cancer? Their model views the nodule from several angles and uses attention to weigh what each view shows, classifying nodules as benign or malignant.

Zhang's multi-view approach helps radiologists sort worrisome nodules from benign ones with greater confidence. Fewer missed cancers and fewer needless biopsies are both wins. Attention maps can also show which views drove the decision, aiding trust. Tools like this are judged by whether they help in real reading rooms, and multi-view designs match how radiologists actually inspect a nodule.
plos-pone-0358063: Mesquita and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on tracking disease outbreaks with digital data. Drawing lessons from past pandemics, the team picked key signals and grouped them with clustering methods. Their aim was nowcasting, a fast estimate of current outbreak levels before official counts land. Strong digital signals can give health officials a head start when a new threat spreads.
plos-pone-0358263:
Esther Su led a team of eight authors reviewing research practice for older adults living with HIV, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their topic was co-design: involving the people a study serves in shaping the study itself. Older adults with HIV are often left out of that planning, even though the research is about them.

Su's group gathered what has been tried and judged how genuine the involvement was. Their review shows that real partnership improves both the quality of studies and the chance that findings get used. For research teams, the message is plain: bring older patients in early as co-creators, not as subjects asked for opinions at the end.
plos-pone-0358363:
Xiaofang Xiong studied young firms and data in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. New ventures now collect large amounts of data but often lack the skill to turn it into advantage. Xiong tested how data capability and fresh business model design work together to shape how well a new venture performs.

The study's core lesson is that data alone does not pay. Returns appear when a firm also reshapes how it creates and captures value, so insight can change offers, prices, or service. Founders reading this gain a warning against buying tools before fixing strategy. Investors, too, can ask sharper questions: not how much data a startup holds, but what its model does with that data.
plos-pone-0358463:
Thomas N Slavens and Hamid Shabgard looked beyond air temperature in building design, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. What bodies actually feel is operative temperature, a blend of air heat and radiant heat from surfaces. The authors explored that fuller measure as a space for finding design ideas borrowed from nature.

Slavens and Shabgard argued that designing for felt temperature can reveal features that air-only targets miss. Nature offers models, from termite mounds to animal coats, for staying comfortable with little energy. Buildings use a huge share of world energy for heating and cooling, so better comfort per unit of energy matters at global scale. The paper reframes an old design variable as a source of fresh ideas.
plos-pone-0358763:
Shih-Han Kao and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on traumatic brain injury. It is a pilot study of blood taken after moderate-to-severe injury. The authors profile methylation of cell-free DNA in blood, chemical marks on DNA fragments that float free in the bloodstream.

Their signatures are enriched for brain cell types, meaning the marks can hint at which brain cells were harmed. A blood test reflecting brain injury could help when scanning is hard or repeated checks are needed. Brain injury specialists and biomarker researchers are the audience for this early test of the idea.
plos-pone-0358863:
Michele Conconi, Raphael Dumas, and Nicola Sancisi rebuild the joints of a leading digital human body model, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The TLEM 2.0 model simulates muscles and bones for movement science, but its knee and ankle were simplified to hinge like connections that let bones drift and overlap unrealistically. The authors reconstructed the true three dimensional motion of four joints, knee, kneecap, and two ankle joints, by maximizing how well the bone surfaces fit together through movement.

From those motions they identified the ligament fibers that stretch least, set the contact points between bones, and defined the model's neutral posture. In the rebuilt chain, bones neither separate nor interpenetrate during motion, and ligaments lengthen in a lifelike pattern. The upgrade sharpens everything the model is used for, from estimating joint forces to designing rehabilitation robots, by making the skeleton move the way skeletons actually do.
plos-pone-0359663:
Nanthida Phattraprayoon, Nut Koonrungsesomboon, and Mingkwan Na Takuathung wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It is a systematic review, with a meta-analysis, of nebulized salbutamol for the fast breathing of newborns whose lung fluid clears slowly, called transient tachypnea. Salbutamol is a standard asthma drug, given here as a mist.

The review weighs efficacy, whether the mist actually shortens the breathing trouble, across the trials done so far. Newborn units need that pooled answer before adopting a drug borrowed from asthma care. Neonatologists deciding treatment for fast-breathing newborns are the readers for this synthesis.
plos-pone-0359863:
Amaraporn Rerkasem and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Set in upper Northern Thailand, it gathers what providers from several professions think about preparing dialysis access in good time. That access, usually a vein and artery joined in the arm, must mature before dialysis can use it.

The study is exploratory and mixed-methods, mixing surveys with interviews across professions. Late access creation forces patients onto temporary catheters, which carry infection risk. Kidney teams in Thailand and similar systems can use providers' own accounts to find where the preparation pathway stalls.
plos-pone-0359963: Jo and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on trauma patients who need very large blood transfusions. The team searched for signs, known right when a patient reaches the emergency room, that predict death. They left out patients with severe brain injury so the signs would reflect bleeding risk alone. The data came from one hospital's past records. Early warning signs help trauma teams act fast.
plos-pone-0360063:
Kapina Mwampembwa and colleagues characterized in 2026 how neutrophils behave in patients with multiple myeloma, a cancer of the plasma cells in bone marrow. Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells and the first responders of the immune system. In myeloma, the cancer and its treatments reshape the immune environment, and neutrophils are part of that story.

Functional characterization means testing what the cells actually do, not only counting them: how they attack microbes, release their contents, and respond to signals. Knowing whether a patient's neutrophils are weakened or overactive could help explain infections and complications that myeloma patients suffer. The study adds cell level evidence from a setting where such detailed immune work is rarely reported.
plos-pone-0360163:
Fang Wang, Jianqiong Li, and Yingjie Shen wrote this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a qualitative evidence synthesis about dementia care supported by artificial intelligence. The people whose views matter here are family and informal caregivers, the unpaid relatives and friends who carry most dementia care.

The synthesis will gather caregivers' acceptance of AI tools, their concerns about them, and what they expect. Planning the review in advance keeps its methods open and checkable. Designers of dementia technology need this caregiver view, since tools that families distrust will sit unused no matter how clever they are.
pmc-13237863: Mice engineered to model ALS and frontotemporal dementia are the subject of a correction notice. The original study built knock-in mice carrying the C9orf72 poly-glycine-alanine change, and reported mild movement test changes and protein shifts matching the human diseases. The correction states that the funding section listed a wrong grant number. Funding numbers tie a paper to the grants that paid for it, and funders audit them, so the journal corrects the record.
pmc-13238263:
Targino and colleagues review the living ecosystem of the mouth and its role in gum disease. Periodontal disease destroys the tissue and bone holding teeth, and remains a leading cause of tooth loss worldwide. Two puzzles persist: many patients struggle to follow treatment routines, and the disease's inner workings are still only partly understood.

The review sets out how bacterial communities on teeth shift from balance to harm, and how the body's response drives much of the damage. That ecological view suggests therapies beyond scraping and antibiotics, such as rebalancing the community itself. For dentists, it reframes gum disease as a disorder of a whole ecosystem, not a single germ.
pmc-13241563:
Zyada and colleagues at Cairo University review the long non-coding RNA XIST and its tangled role in breast cancer. XIST normally silences one X chromosome in female cells. The review traces how it interacts with microRNAs, transcription factors, and signaling pathways inside tumors. Its effects reach drug resistance, the tumor surroundings, and cancer stem cells.

Crucially, XIST does not behave the same in every breast cancer subtype. It often promotes tumors, yet in some luminal and triple-negative settings its role looks more restraining. That split personality complicates any single reading of its levels. The authors still see promise in XIST as a diagnostic marker, a prognostic sign, and a drug target.
pmc-13243163:
Elyor Berdimurodov and colleagues reviewed five years of progress in turning plant waste into glowing sensor particles. Their review appeared in Bioresources and Bioprocessing in 2026. Carbon quantum dots cooked from fruit peels, leaves, and farm waste fluoresce brightly and cost little to make. Between 2021 and 2025, researchers refined recipes using heated water, microwaves, and pyrolysis, sometimes finishing in ten minutes.

The dots come out a few nanometers wide, partly graphitic, and their glow can be tuned by what they are made from and what they are doped with. Sensors built on them detect iron at extremely low levels, spot antibiotics through glow changes, and catch farm and household chemicals such as glyphosate, ammonia, and formaldehyde. Selectivity and sensitivity rival conventional quantum dots without the toxic metals. The authors call biomass dots a sustainable platform ready for wider sensing use. Remaining work centers on standardization and real-world samples.
pmc-13244563:
Ngoc Hai Tran and colleagues present a five-step surgical technique, named DARIP, for the deadliest form of placenta accreta in mid-pregnancy. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2026. A thirty-five-year-old woman at nearly twenty-two weeks arrived with vaginal bleeding, and ultrasound showed placenta percreta, where the placenta grows through the uterine wall. In low-resource settings, removing the uterus is not the safest answer.

The procedure works through five moves. It clears the bladder-uterus plane of new vessels, drains amniotic fluid, and places a rectangle of blood-stopping stitches. Only then does it cut the uterus, through the blocked-off zone, and sew the placental bed. The authors call DARIP promising for second-trimester disease and share a video of the operation. They insist it belongs in expert centers and needs testing in larger series before adoption.
pmc-13244963:
Laura Kim and colleagues tested pressurized oxygen for ME/CFS, an exhausting illness with no approved therapy. Their study appeared in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2026. Thirty patients, mostly women in their early forties, completed forty hyperbaric oxygen sessions. The team tracked functioning, fatigue, pain, exercise capacity, grip strength, thinking speed, and standing tolerance. Brains were scanned before and after, against thirty healthy controls.

Physical functioning, the main outcome, improved meaningfully during treatment, and pain and fatigue scores fell by clinically important margins. Patients also exercised longer, gripped harder, and processed information faster after the sessions. Brain scans showed the thalamus's connection pattern shifting toward the healthy profile, and that shift tracked who responded. Treatment was well tolerated. The authors link the benefit to correcting disturbed thalamus function. Without a placebo arm the proof stays early, but the signal spans symptoms, performance, and brain measures alike.
pmc-13245763:
Zhang, Sun, Chen, and co-authors optimized the water passages of a large drainage pumping station in this 2026 PLOS One engineering study. Vertical mixed-flow pumps move floodwater at scale, and badly shaped intake and discharge passages waste energy and destabilize flow. Traditional tuning changes one factor at a time; instead, the team combined orthogonal experimental design, which tests factor combinations efficiently, with computational fluid dynamics simulations.

Their scoring system weighed hydraulic loss, flow uniformity, and inflow angle together. The winning intake design kept losses tiny and delivered nearly perfectly uniform, near-vertical inflow, while the discharge design flowed smoothly without separation and fit the station's layout. A physical model test confirmed the predictions, reaching strong efficiency at the design point with simulation and experiment agreeing closely.
pmc-13247263:
Guo and colleagues tested a two-drug combination against advanced head and neck cancer in this 2026 phase 1b/2 trial in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Patients received toripalimab, an immune checkpoint drug, plus cetuximab, an antibody blocking a growth receptor. One group had already failed platinum chemotherapy; another, selected for a positive PD-L1 marker, was previously untreated. Eighty-eight patients enrolled across several centers.

Tumors shrank in sixty percent of the platinum-resistant group and about forty-four percent of the untreated group, with median survival around fourteen and eighteen months respectively. Patients whose tumors scored positive for PD-L1 benefited more. Severe side effects affected roughly half of patients, but no new safety problems appeared. The authors call the pairing promising for a cancer with few good options.
pmc-13248263:
Lai and colleagues followed two hundred children wearing overnight corneal reshaping lenses, in a 2026 BMC Ophthalmology study. These lenses slow worsening eyesight in myopia, and the team compared a smaller optical zone design against a larger one. Children aged seven to twelve were grouped by both lens type and starting prescription strength.

After one year, eyes grew least in the group pairing moderate myopia with the smaller zone. That group also had the highest share of children whose myopia did not progress. The authors conclude the smaller design controls myopia better, especially for children who start with milder prescriptions.
pmc-13248463:
Guo and colleagues grew sheep womb-lining organoids in the lab, reported in Veterinary Research in 2026. The luminal epithelium is the surface where an embryo first meets the mother, and flat cell cultures fail to copy its structure. The team built three-dimensional organoids from that surface layer using a tuned growth medium.

The organoids showed the right markers, secreted mucin, and answered hormones much like real tissue. Turned inside out, they matched the womb's natural orientation, and embryos placed with them grew and spread better. Gene readings confirmed a close match to native lining. The authors offer the system for studying pregnancy recognition and fertility treatments in livestock.
pmc-13248963:
Maswanganyi and colleagues tested a rapid blood infection panel in Limpopo, South Africa, reported in 2026. Bloodstream infections kill many patients, and remote labs often wait long for conventional identification. The team ran two hundred forty-seven positive blood cultures through both the BioFire BCID2 panel and the standard VITEK2 system at a routine laboratory.

The rapid panel matched the standard closely, with sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy all above ninety-five percent. About a quarter of samples held more than one microbe, and the panel also flagged drug resistance genes, most often one linked to broad antibiotic resistance. The authors recommend the panel where fast answers can change treatment.
pmc-13249963: Scientific Reports retracted this 2025 article in 2026, and this note records the withdrawal. Chandra and colleagues had used machine learning to predict the compressive strength of polymer-infused bricks, with SHAP analysis to explain the model. Editors later found the paper overlapped substantially with an earlier submitted, then withdrawn, manuscript that shared only two authors. The authors could not adequately explain the authorship change, given the stated contributions. The editors therefore lost confidence in the article's integrity and retracted it.
pmc-13250863:
Han, Wu, and Wu compare two antibiotic-loaded materials for treating long-standing bone infections. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine study covers two hundred forty-four patients with chronic osteomyelitis treated between 2017 and 2024. One group received vancomycin in bone cement alone, and the other an added calcium sulfate carrier holding the same drug.

The combined material controlled infection in about seven of eight patients, versus roughly three of four with cement alone. Reoperations and overall complications both fell sharply in the combined group. Blood inflammation markers also dropped further, and quality-of-life scores for physical health and energy ran higher. The authors judge the combination a promising upgrade for this stubborn infection, worth wider clinical use.
pmc-13251763:
Tsotetsi, Nkoana, and Khan review a structured dry eye diagnosis system and its scarce use in African clinics. Their 2026 Clinical Optometry paper covers the JENVIS Pro Dry Eye Report, a software report paired with a corneal imaging device. Dry eye disease troubles the eye surface with unstable tears, discomfort, and blurred vision.

Seventy sources fed the review of disease patterns, risk factors, and diagnostic methods. The JENVIS system combines objective tear measures with symptom scores and proved reliable and reproducible in the literature. African studies still lean on older tests such as the Schirmer strip and dye break-up timing. The authors advocate wider JENVIS adoption in Africa to standardize diagnosis, teach patients, and guide evidence-based care.
pmc-13255063:
Zhao, Chen, and Wang present a lab protocol for detecting protein S-glutathionylation in the model plant Arabidopsis during stress. This reversible change helps govern protein stability and signaling, but its fragile disulfide bonds break easily and samples oxidize after harvest, so direct checks in living tissue have been shaky. The method uses no transgenic plants.

Instead, a chemical toolkit tags proteins through propargyl glycine feeding and click chemistry. The protocol covers whole-proteome counting, pulling out tagged targets for western blotting or tandem mass spectrometry, and imaging the change in place. Step-by-step steps make the workflow easy for other plant labs to adopt.
pmc-13259263:
Ramya Shekhar and a large Indian team hunt the best tomato lines for greenhouse growing. Indeterminate types, which keep climbing and fruiting, suit off-season protected production. Their 2026 trial grew fifty-seven genotypes for two years and scored sixteen yield and quality traits.

Every trait varied significantly across the lines. Fruit weight and fruits per cluster looked directly selectable, being highly heritable with strong expected gains. Grouping split the lines into seven clusters, each championing earliness, nutrition, or fruit size. A multi-trait index crowned three elite genotypes, named PIDGT-39, PIDGT-42, and PIDGT-29. Breeders now have parent stock shortcuts from this work.
pmc-13262263:
Larissa Ringelstetter and colleagues uncover a brake on the cell's low-oxygen alarm that works without its usual tools. RNF8 normally tags proteins for disposal, while HIF1α rallies genes when oxygen runs short. Their 2026 study shows RNF8 quietly opposing a rival protein that protects HIF1α in hypoxia.

Surprisingly, RNF8's tagging power was irrelevant to the effect. Instead, its forkhead-associated domain gripped the tail of HIF1α directly, shown by yeast two-hybrid tests. The grip held even when HIF1α could not be hydroxylated, the usual oxygen signal. This hidden association could matter for hypoxia-driven cancers like triple-negative breast cancer.
pmc-13262563:
Hao Tang and colleagues review the conversation between prostate cancer and the bone it invades. Prostate tumors in bone usually provoke extra bone building, orchestrated by resident bone cells. Their 2026 review weighs each cell type's contribution to that corrupt remodeling.

Bone-eating cells start the cycle but blocking them helps patients surprisingly little. Bone-building cells can either lull tumors to sleep or whip them into aggressive change, depending on signals. Osteocytes, bone's most numerous cells, release pro-invasion messengers when mechanical sensing shifts. Tumor exosomes reprogram the whole neighborhood in return. Breaking this self-reinforcing loop is the therapeutic prize.
pmc-13318363:
Eren and colleagues measure the strain on family caregivers of dying patients with pressure injuries in this 2026 study. Pressure injuries are painful wounds from lying in one position, common in palliative care. Unpaid relatives provide much of the daily care. The team surveyed caregivers at a state hospital using a burden interview and a social support scale.

The study covered 138 caregivers, who reported a high level of burden overall. Burden ran higher for caregivers with lower income, those who found care tasks difficult, and those whose family and social life suffered. Feeling well supported by others went with lower burden, suggesting support protects caregivers. Eren argues that services for these patients should treat caregiver support as essential, not optional.
pmc-13338663:
Puig-Esteve and Morrison mapped the literature in 2026 on occupational resilience, the idea that taking part in meaningful daily activities helps people adapt and recover through hardship.
