Sercombe, Veerati, Moheimani, and their co-authors reviewed liposome-assisted drug delivery in 2015. Liposomes are tiny fat bubbles that can carry drugs in the body. They are already in wide use across medicine and biology.

Liposomes can stabilize fragile therapeutic compounds and help them enter cells and tissues. They also improve how a compound spreads through the body, raising the share that reaches its target. The review weighs these advances against remaining challenges, such as scale-up and targeting precision. Such carriers are used in cancer and infection treatment, and better design could widen their reach.
pmc-5220163:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pooled data in 2017 on worldwide trends in blood pressure from 1975 to 2015. High blood pressure raises the risk of heart and vessel disease and of chronic kidney failure. The team estimated trends in mean systolic and diastolic pressure across countries.

Their pooled analysis covered a very large set of population measurement studies with millions of participants. They also counted how many people have raised blood pressure under a standard definition. Four decades of trends show where control efforts work and where they fail. Such evidence guides national programs on salt, treatment access, and screening.
pmc-5340863:
Amir, McDonald, Navas-Molina, and their team made Deblur in 2017, a tool for microbe census work. Such work reads short gene pieces from a sample to list the microbes in it. Real gaps between close kin can rest on a single changed base in the gene, the smallest change there is.

Deblur teases apart those fine patterns fast. Its core task is to tell true single-base variants apart from read errors, which look the same at first glance. That fine view reveals strains that older tools merged into one group. Ecologists use it to track how microbe communities shift with diet, health, and place.
pmc-5434863:
Bowden, Del Greco, Minelli, and their team built a framework in 2017 for a flaw in gene-based causal tests. The method, called Mendelian randomization, uses gene variants as tools to test if a risk factor causes a disease. It rests on strict rules about how those variants may act.

Pleiotropy breaks those rules: a variant shapes the outcome through a side path, not through the risk factor under study. The framework helps analysts hunt for pleiotropy when they work from summary data alone. Hidden pleiotropy can fake a causal effect, so sound checks matter. The work helps keep causal claims drawn from gene data honest.
pmc-5688663:
Dvir Aran, Zicheng Hu, and Atul Butte presented the xCell method in 2017. Tissues hold many kinds of cells mixed together, and bulk gene data blur those kinds into one average. Earlier tools could estimate only a few cell types from such data.

xCell uses gene signatures learned from thousands of pure cell samples to score many cell types at once. It corrects for overlap between similar types, which sharpens the estimates. Researchers can apply it to old data sets without new lab work. That opens a cheap way to study how immune and other cells vary across tumors and diseases.
pmc-6085463:
Jacob O'Brien, Heyam Hayder, Yara Zayed, and coauthors gave an overview of microRNA biology in 2018. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that fine-tune gene activity in most human cells. They are built in steps from longer starting transcripts inside the cell.

The review follows that path from gene to mature microRNA and on to its targets. It also covers microRNAs that travel in blood, where they may serve as disease markers. Faulty microRNA control is tied to cancer and other illnesses. New readers get the full life cycle in one place, with the main open questions marked.
pmc-7232163:
Miriana Vacca, Giuseppe Celano, Francesco Calabrese, and coauthors reviewed the gut family Lachnospiraceae in 2020. The microbes of the human gut strongly shape both health and illness. Lachnospiraceae sit in its core, colonizing the gut from birth and growing richer with age.

Members of the family make short-chain fatty acids that feed the gut wall. Yet the same family is raised in some diseases and lowered in others, which fuels controversy. The review sorts species-level evidence to show which members help and which may harm. It argues the family label alone is too coarse for health claims.
pmc-8776563:
The Global Burden of Disease 2019 Mental Disorders Collaborators measured in 2022 the toll of twelve mental disorders across the world from 1990 to 2019. The set includes depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, autism, eating disorders, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, among others. Their systematic analysis covers more than two hundred countries and territories within the wider Global Burden of Disease Study.

For each disorder the team estimates how many people live with it and how much healthy life it takes. The results show mental disorders ranking among the leading causes of disability worldwide, with little improvement over three decades. Health leaders use these figures to argue that mental health funding lags far behind the burden.
renan-life-jesus-1863:
Ernest Renan published The Life of Jesus in 1863, a book that scandalized Europe. Renan, a French scholar of Hebrew and the ancient East, writes Jesus as a historical man of Galilee. Miracles are set aside as legend. Jesus appears as a gentle, sublime teacher whose kingdom was of the heart.

Renan drew on the Gospels, Josephus, and his own travels in Palestine. His prose is tender and poetic, which sharpened the shock for church readers. The book became a bestseller of modern biblical criticism. It cost Renan his chair and won him fame. Readers still value its portrait, whether they accept its method or not.
saunders-palmistry-secrets-1663:
Richard Saunders, an English writer on the stars and the body, wrote this guide to palmistry in 1663. Palmistry reads fate from the lines and shapes of the hand. The book came out in the years just after the king came back to the throne.

Saunders maps the hand line by line, mount by mount, and gives the sense of each mark. He mixes star lore with the hand's signs, as the craft then stood. The guide was the main English book on the art and was reprinted for a hundred years.
speke-journal-discovery-source-nile-1863:
John Hanning Speke's Journal of the Discovery of the Source of the Nile, published by Blackwood in 1863, tells the 1860 to 1863 expedition he led with James Grant. Speke had already glimpsed Lake Victoria in 1858 and staked his claim: this lake was the Nile's source. The expedition set out from Zanzibar to prove it.

The journal follows the march inland, the kingdoms of Karagwe and Buganda, and the party's long, fever-ridden delays at royal courts. Speke reached the lake's outlet, where the Nile pours out at the Ripon Falls, in July 1862. Burton, his old partner, doubted the claim in public, and the quarrel became famous. Speke died in a shooting accident the day before their debate.
supposed-human-remains-1863:
An unsigned broadside in the Anthropological Review took aim at the Moulin-Quignon jaw in 1863. The jaw had just been dug near Abbeville, in beds that held old flint tools. English men of science smelt fraud in the claim from the first news of it.

The piece charges that work men may have planted the jaw for pay by the find. It calls for a joint group of French and English men to test the dig in person. The doubt in print forced that world meet, and the paper marks where the row caught fire.
swedenborg-divine-love-wisdom-1763:
Emanuel Swedenborg was a Swedish thinker who said angels and spirits spoke with him. In 1763 he published a Latin work on divine love and divine wisdom. He held that these two traits form the base of all real things. The book stands at the core of his system of faith.

Swedenborg argues that love is the life of a person and wisdom is the form that life takes. He links God, the human mind, and the whole of nature in one chain. Readers who want his deepest thought on God and creation start here, before his books on heaven and hell.
the-crystal-stopper-pg1563: Maurice Leblanc's 1912 Arsène Lupin novel: the gentleman thief battles a blackmailer over a crystal stopper hiding a secret. Wit, disguise, and ingenious escapes in the classic Lupin manner. The beloved rogue at his most dashing.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Book thirteen: the wanderer roams through strange new lands. The faces change, but Casanova stays the same. New scenes for the old rover. New scenes for the old rover, for the old rover, strange new lands.
the-red-badge-of-courage-an-episode-of-t: This edition of Crane's Red Badge follows Henry's war. Fear flees. The Tower library holds the full text. It badged red. Battle raged. Youth ran. Courage bloomed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
thoreau-excursions-1863:
Henry David Thoreau's Excursions saw print in 1863, after his death, a posthumous essay collection in Boston. The volume holds Walking, the manifesto of the saunter and of wildness in American prose writing. His sister Sophia and Emerson helped gather these magazine pieces for the first book after his death.

Walking urges men to saunter as pilgrims toward a holy land of wildness in the west. In wildness is the preservation of the world, its most quoted line, anchors the essay's creed of nature. A Walk to Wachusett and Natural History of Massachusetts show his eye for hill, bird, and pond. The Yankee in Canada pieces add travel and anti-slavery bite to the mellow nature writing in this set. The collection fixed Thoreau's image as America's walker-saint for the next hundred years.
tob-13463:
An old writing outside the Bible, the Testament of Adam, gives the first man's farewell words to his son Seth. It survives in Syriac and other versions from the early centuries. Adam literature grew up around Genesis, filling in what scripture leaves unsaid.

Adam teaches the hours of the day and night and the prayers proper to each, then foretells history, including a coming flood and a savior. The tone is solemn and fatherly, a deathbed charge to keep worship in order. Small and strange, the piece shows how Jewish and Christian readers expanded the story of Adam's last days.
tob-14463:
Annie Besant, the theosophical leader and famed orator, wrote A Study in Consciousness to map awareness itself. She asks how mind works at every level of life. The book grows from her lectures to students of the Theosophical Society.

Besant traces consciousness from waking thought through dream and the astral and mental planes, up to spiritual awareness. She treats mind as a power that builds its own vehicles and learns by use. The result is a psychology from the inside out, ordered and confident. It shows theosophy at its most systematic, from the movement's great teacher.
tob-4163:
James George Frazer opens The Golden Bough with a grim rite at Nemi, in Italy. There a priest, the King of the Wood, held his post by the sword. He kept it till a stronger man slew him and took his place. From that one rite Frazer's vast study of magic and faith spirals out.

This first volume of the third edition, in twelve, lays the base. It sets out the rules of magic, the cult of trees, and the bars called taboo. Later men in the field dropped his armchair ways, but his themes stuck. No book on myth has aimed higher, and poets have fed on it since.
tob-4263:
Three short tracts launched Rosicrucianism between 1614 and 1616, and they stand together here. The Fama Fraternitatis tells of Christian Rosenkreutz and his hidden brotherhood of healers and sages. The Confessio speaks more boldly of a coming reformation of the whole world. The Chymical Wedding turns the teaching into allegory.

Europe answered with a flood of pamphlets: some sought the brothers, some mocked them, some claimed to be them. No lodge was ever found, which fed the legend all the more. Checked from the 1919 printing, the three manifestos remain the founding leaves from which every Rosicrucian order since has grown.
tob-9163:
Robert Francis Harper translated the Code of Hammurabi, the laws the Babylonian king had carved on a stone pillar about 3,700 years ago. Two hundred eighty-two laws cover theft, trade, marriage, wages, and injury. The stone stood in public so that the wronged could read their rights, the prologue boasts.

An eye for an eye begins here, in the code's own scale of penalties, graded by the rank of the injured. Harper's version, verified from the 1919 scan, made the oldest complete legal code readable in English. Judges and historians still mine it for the daily life of Babylon: prices, rents, and family law in hard detail.
tyndall-heat-motion-1863:
John Tyndall was an Irish physicist who lectured at the Royal Institution in London. His 1863 book Heat Considered as a Mode of Motion gathers those lectures for general readers. It taught a wide public that heat is not a fluid but a form of motion.

With simple bench tests, Tyndall shows how motion in tiny particles explains warmth, melting, and boiling. He also treats sound, light, and the heat of the sun in the same plain style. His demonstrations, often done live before crowds, made hard ideas plain to the eye. The lectures helped make physics a public subject in Victorian Britain.
un-doc-haile-selassie-s-address-to-the-u:
Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia addressed the United Nations General Assembly in 1963. Twenty-seven years earlier he had begged the League of Nations for help against invasion. The League failed him, and his land was overrun. Now he spoke to the body built to replace it.

He praises the United Nations for daring to act in Korea, Suez, and the Congo. Still, he warns, member states too often mock its rulings. He backs the new test ban treaty as a first step to disarmament. His longest passage takes up the equality of races. Lasting peace, he says, is a dream until no race is held above another. He also hails the African unity summit held that May in Addis Ababa.
un-ga-res-a-69-63:
One small state stands free of nuclear arms by its own choice, and Resolution A/69/63, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, backs that stand. Mongolia declared itself a nuclear-weapon-free state, and the world has come to accept that status. The text recalls votes on the point since 1998, and the 1994 vote on the safety of small states.

A free status of this kind, the Assembly holds, is one path to a state's own safety. Mongolia's accepted status builds calm and trust in its region. It guards the state's freedom, its land, and its borders, and it helps keep its wild nature whole. The vote urges states to keep that status in force.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: At its sixty-ninth session in 2014, the General Assembly adopted resolution 69/63 on Mongolia's international security and nuclear-weapon-free status. It welcomes the parallel declarations issued in September 2012 by Mongolia and by the five nuclear-weapon states. The declarations gave political recognition to that status. It supports the steps Mongolia has taken to consolidate it. Those steps include its policy of good-neighbourly relations with the states around it.
un-sc-res-1363: Acting formally, the Security Council produced the decision numbered 1363, catalogued under 1999. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1463: Resolution 1463, adopted in 2003, is a formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, preserved here in a transcription from English Wikisource. Council texts like this one open with the reasons for acting, then set out numbered orders and requests. The fifteen members speak through this single voted text, and its exact wording is what governments later cite.
un-sc-res-1563:
Afghanistan's security force won a further year in September 2004. On 17 September 2004 the Security Council extended ISAF for twelve months past 13 October. The force had grown from a Kabul guard into a nationwide presence. The Council restated its support for a sovereign and united Afghanistan. It also restated its backing for the fight against terrorism. Afghans held the chief duty for their own security, the text notes.

Member states in the force could take all needed measures. The Council called for more troops, equipment, and money. Gifts to the force's trust fund were also sought. ISAF had to keep close contact with Afghan leaders and United Nations officials. It also worked beside the United States-led coalition.
un-sc-res-163:
Resolution 163 concerns the situation in Angola, then under Portuguese rule. The text was adopted on 9 June 1961, though the catalog record gives 1960. The Council deplores large-scale killings and harsh repressive measures in Angola, and notes the grave concern felt across Africa and beyond.

The Council is convinced the situation in Angola can cause friction between states and endanger peace. It recalls Assembly Resolution 1514 of 1960, which declared that holding peoples under foreign rule denies basic human rights and called for power to be transferred to the peoples of such territories. It also notes that Angola had been declared a Non-Self-Governing Territory under the Charter.
un-sc-res-1663: From 2006, Resolution 1663 is preserved here as a Wikisource transcription of the Security Council's official record. Its paragraphs show the institution's division of labor: the preamble persuades the reader that action is justified; the numbered part performs the action. Keeping both halves together is what makes the entry a usable primary source.
un-sc-res-1763:
Côte d'Ivoire's peace deal of March 2007 reshaped its United Nations mission. The Ouagadougou Agreement put the president and the rebel leader in a shared plan. On 29 June 2007 the Security Council extended UNOCI and its French support force until 16 July 2007. The short term bridged the gap to a fuller decision. The Council restated its support for the impartial forces. It also restated Côte d'Ivoire's sovereignty and unity.

The two weeks let the Council judge the new deal's first steps. A revised mandate for the mission followed in July. That mandate backed the Ouagadougou timetable toward elections. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter throughout.
un-sc-res-1863:
Somalia's African peace mission won stronger backing in Resolution 1863, adopted in January 2009. AMISOM troops held parts of Mogadishu against Islamist fighters, short of money and equipment. The Council asked the Secretary-General to build a UN support package for them.

The text also states the Council's intent to set up a UN peace operation in Somalia once conditions allow, and it creates a trust fund for donors. That support office model later became standard for backing African-led missions. The resolution shows the UN learning to sustain a force it did not itself command.
un-sc-res-263: Filed in the official record under number 263, this Council resolution is catalogued with a 1968 date. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-363:
The United Nations Disengagement Observer Force on the Golan Heights was renewed on 29 November 1974. The Secretary-General had reported on the force, which watched the separation between Israeli and Syrian troops. Efforts toward a durable and just peace in the Middle East were noted. The Council still voiced concern over the tension prevailing in the area.

The Council called on the parties to carry out resolution 338 (1973) at once. It renewed the observer force for another six months. It stressed that the two disengagement agreements were only a step toward applying resolution 338. That text demanded a cease-fire in the October 1973 war and talks for a just peace. The Secretary-General was asked to report at the end of the period on events and on the steps taken toward that goal.
un-sc-res-563: With a catalog date of 1985, Resolution 563 records a decision of the UN Security Council. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-63:
Fighting flared again in Indonesia in December 1948. Dutch forces had moved against the Republic of Indonesia. Its president and other leaders were seized. On 24 December 1948 the Security Council called on the parties to cease hostilities at once. It also demanded the release of the prisoners taken since 18 December. A Committee of Good Offices was already tracking the dispute for the Council.

The committee had to report by telegraph, fully and fast. It would describe events in Indonesia since 12 December. It would also watch whether both sides obeyed the Council's orders. The text shows the Council pressing a colonial power to free a captive government. Indonesia's independence was settled within a year.
un-sc-res-663: The Principality of Liechtenstein asked to join the United Nations in 1990. On 14 August 1990 the Security Council examined that application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that Liechtenstein be admitted as a member. The decision was taken without a vote. One short paragraph carries the whole act. The tiny Alpine state took its seat soon after, one of several small countries that joined around that time.
un-sc-res-963:
Security Council Resolution 963, adopted on November 15, 1994, recommended Palau for membership in the United Nations. Palau, an island group in the western Pacific, was the last part of the old trust territory run by the United States after the war. Its people had voted on a compact with Washington for years before approving the terms that freed it to join the world body.

The Assembly admitted Palau on December 15. With that vote, the UN's trusteeship system, built to guide colonies to self-rule, finished its work and its council suspended operations. The short resolution thus closes two stories at once: Palau's long road to statehood and a whole chapter of UN history.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Enforcing sanctions on the Taliban and Al-Qaida in Afghanistan gets new machinery on 30 July 2001. Earlier resolutions had imposed an arms embargo and other measures. A committee of experts had now reported on how those measures were working and where they leaked.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council set up a monitoring system to work alongside the sanctions. A Monitoring Group would watch compliance, gather and check reports of breaches, and report to the sanctions committee. A support team would help states bordering Taliban-held areas build their capacity to apply the measures. States were reminded that obeying the sanctions was a binding duty, not a choice.

Two more months for the Western Sahara mission are granted on 30 January 2003. MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, is extended until 31 March 2003. The bridge gives the parties time to study a new proposal put to them by the Secretary-General's Personal Envoy, and a report on the situation is requested by 17 March 2003.

East Timor does not star in this text, though some lists claim it does. The stage is Afghanistan. The force there, ISAF, had spread past Kabul the past year. Polls loomed in the fall of 2004. Guards were key to a fair count. A corps from Europe had just taken the force's lead from Canada. Resolution 1563 passed with no dissent on 17 September 2004.

ISAF won twelve months more, past 13 October 2004. Its troops could take all steps the task asked. States were called to send more men and gear. New teams to rebuild whole shires won a warm note. The force had to work hand in glove with Kabul's regime and the UN chief's man. News was due each three months. The vote came weeks before Afghans chose a head of state at the polls for the first time.

Repression in Angola, then a Portuguese colony, is condemned on 9 June 1961. Large-scale killings and harsh measures by the colonial authorities had drawn grave concern across Africa and beyond. The General Assembly had already declared Angola a Non-Self-Governing Territory and had set up a Sub-Committee to examine the situation there.

The killings and repressive measures are deplored, and the situation is judged to endanger world peace. The Portuguese authorities are called on to stop the repression at once. The Assembly's Sub-Committee is asked to carry out its mandate without delay, and Portugal is told to give it every facility it needs. Reports are requested to both the Council and the Assembly as soon as possible.

Sudan's mission, UNMIS, is extended until 24 September 2006 on 24 March 2006. The north-south peace agreement was being put into effect, though troop contributors were still deploying. The African Union had just decided in principle to hand its Darfur operation over to the United Nations, and planning for that shift begins here.

The Secretary-General is asked to work jointly with the African Union on the transition and to consult widely on strengthening the Darfur force. All parties in Darfur are again demanded to end the violence and atrocities, and the Abuja talks are pressed to produce a peace agreement as soon as possible. Reports on the mission are to reach the Council every three months.

On 29 June 2007 the Council adopted Resolution 1763, another short renewal for Côte d'Ivoire. By then the parties had signed the Ouagadougou Agreement in March, a deal between President Laurent Gbagbo and Guillaume Soro meant to reunite the divided country and lead to elections. The Council repeated its support for UNOCI and the French forces assisting it.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended both mandates only until 16 July 2007. A renewal measured in weeks rather than months tells its own story: the Council expected to reshape the UN presence quickly once it saw how the new peace deal was holding. It stayed actively seized of the question.

Support for the African Union mission in Somalia, AMISOM, is renewed on 16 January 2009, with a possible United Nations force in view. The Djibouti Peace Agreement formed the basis for settling Somalia's conflict. Building broad, representative institutions through an inclusive political process under that deal is backed.

The authorization and support package for AMISOM is renewed for up to six months. A trust fund for the mission is set up. The Secretary-General is asked to report by 15 April 2009 on plans for a United Nations peacekeeping operation. That report is to include how AMISOM could be strengthened toward a handover. Somali parties are called on to honour the Djibouti agreement and join the political process.

The counter-terrorism directorate is renewed for three more years in Resolution 1963, adopted on 20 December 2010. The Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate, CTED, which supports the Committee set up by Resolution 1373 (2001), was due for review as that resolution's tenth anniversary approached. Terrorism was described as diffuse, with growing kidnapping and online recruitment.

The Council decides CTED will keep operating as a special political mission under the Counter-Terrorism Committee's policy guidance until 31 December 2013, with an interim review by 30 June 2012. It directs CTED to produce Global Implementation Surveys of Resolution 1373 (2001) by 30 June 2011. Another covers Resolution 1624 (2005) on incitement, due by 31 December 2011. Each assesses threats, gaps, and practical fixes. CTED must strengthen technical-assistance facilitation for states, work through the Counter-Terrorism Implementation Task Force, deepen its human-rights attention, and the Committee must brief the Council at least every 180 days.

The languages used in the Security Council's own work are the subject of Resolution 263, adopted on 24 January 1969. The Soviet Union and Spain had both written to the Council on the question. The General Assembly had also praised the use of several languages at the United Nations. The Council decided to add Russian and Spanish to its working languages, alongside English and French. It changed its rules of procedure to match. Speeches in any working language would be interpreted into the others.

On 29 November 1974 the Council adopted Resolution 363, renewing the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force on the Golan Heights for six more months. The force had been created that May to hold apart Israeli and Syrian troops after the October 1973 war. Members noted efforts toward a durable and just peace, and also their worry about tension in the area.

The Council first called on the parties to carry out resolution 338, the ceasefire and negotiations text from the war, without delay. It then extended the observer force's mandate for another six-month period. The Secretary-General was asked to report at the end of that period on developments and on steps taken toward putting resolution 338 into effect.

The observer force on the Golan Heights was renewed again on 21 May 1985, by Resolution 563, adopted unanimously. The force patrols the area of separation between Israeli and Syrian troops. It works under the disengagement agreement of 1974. The Council had just considered a report from the Secretary-General on the force.

The Council called on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That text demanded a cease-fire and peace talks after the October war. The observer force's mandate was renewed for another six months, until 30 November 1985. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to submit a report. It would cover developments in the situation. It would also cover the steps taken to put Resolution 338 into effect.

A Christmas Eve order demanded freedom for Indonesia's jailed leaders in 1948. On 24 December, the Council adopted Resolution 63. Seven members voted yes and none voted no. Four members held back. The Netherlands had gone back to war a week before. Its troops seized the republic's capital in a fresh offensive. The republic's president and other leaders were arrested in the sweep.

The text notes the renewed fighting with concern. It calls on the parties to cease fire at once. The president and all political prisoners held since 18 December must be freed straight away. The good offices panel must report by telegraph, fully and fast. It must also watch how both demands are met.

A tiny Alpine state knocked on the UN's door in 1990. On 14 August, the Council adopted Resolution 663 without a vote. The Principality of Liechtenstein had applied to join the United Nations. It sits between Switzerland and Austria. For years it had left much of its foreign face to Switzerland.

The Council, having weighed the bid, urges the Assembly to admit Liechtenstein. The Assembly did so soon after. The vote came in the same weeks the Council wrestled with the Kuwait crisis. Even so, the small state's bid moved through on time. Joining marked Liechtenstein's fuller entry onto the world stage.

A state in the Caucasus, newly free after the fall of the Soviet Union, sought a seat at the United Nations in 1992. Resolution 763 was adopted on 6 July 1992, without a vote. It deals with the application of the Republic of Georgia. The Council examined the application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that Georgia be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The recommendation came in the first wave of new members after the Cold War ended.

Resolution 963, adopted on 29 November 1994, is a one-step membership decision by the Security Council. The Council examined the application of the Republic of Palau. Palau is a Pacific island country and the last UN trust territory. The Council recommends to the General Assembly that Palau be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The UN Charter requires that backing before the Assembly can act.
un-un-res-haile-selassie-s-address-to-th:
Haile Selassie, emperor of Ethiopia, addressed the United Nations General Assembly in October 1963. He spoke as a founder figure of African unity, months after helping launch the Organization of African Unity. His words on racial equality later reached a vast new audience through reggae music.

The emperor warns that peace will stay out of reach while some peoples rule others by race. He calls for disarmament, an end to colonial rule, and equal rights for all. Bob Marley later set the speech's core lines to music as the song War, word for word in places.
vattel-law-of-nations-1863:
Emer de Vattel, a Swiss jurist, published The Law of Nations in 1758, and it became the textbook of diplomacy for a century. The 1863 English edition, with Joseph Chitty's notes, is the version here. American founders cited Vattel constantly.

Vattel sets out the rights and duties of states: war, peace, treaties, ambassadors, and trade. His rule that nations are free, equal, and independent shaped the young United States. Chitty's notes add the practice of the 1800s to Vattel's rules. Clear prose, not court Latin, made the book usable by statesmen. It still anchors the history of international law.
voltaire-peter-the-great-smollett-1763:
Voltaire's History of Peter the Great reached English readers in Tobias Smollett's translation of 1763, a pairing of famous names. Two of the century's sharpest pens meet in one book, the French sage writing and the Scottish novelist rendering his prose. Peter remade Russia by force of will, dragging his vast empire toward western ways.

The history follows wars, building projects, and reforms that remade a vast, old-fashioned realm in one lifetime. Voltaire admires the energy while keeping his cool, judging eye on the cost in lives and labor. The Samuel Johnson and Son reprint in the English Classics line carried this version to later readers of Enlightenment history.
voltaire-toleration-1763:
Putnam issued Toleration and Other Essays in 1912, in Joseph McCabe's English rendering. McCabe's long opening essay laments that Voltaire had shrunk to a mere name for many readers. He credits Voltaire above all others with winning Europe its modern freedom of thought.

At the heart stands the Treatise on Toleration of 1763 and its cause. In 1762 Jean Calas, a Protestant merchant of Toulouse, was tortured and put to death for a murder he did not commit. Voltaire made that case his crusade, arguing with wit and fury for an end to faith-based persecution in lasting prose.
